For this exercise you will use voles_metabolism.csv, a small synthetic biological dataset deliberately chosen because its column names are unlikely to feature in Copilot’s training data. The columns are subject_id, sex, treatment_arm, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g, and metabolic_rate_post. The data record a hypothetical metabolism trial in voles with three treatment arms and two sexes, sample size 72.
1. Start with no context. Open a blank R script. Type only this single comment into your script, then wait:

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment

Record what Copilot suggests. With no library() call, no data loaded, and no column names visible, Copilot has to guess. It will produce something syntactically plausible but most likely wrong for your dataset, because it does not know what your columns are called.
2. Restart with full context. Start a new blank script. Add the following at the top:

# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
# 72 voles, three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose), two sexes
# Native pipe |>, tidyverse

library(tidyverse)

voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
glimpse(voles)

Then add the same comment as before, on a new line:

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment

Record what Copilot suggests this time. The expected output resembles:


Solution


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(
    mean_change = mean(mass_change_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = treatment_arm
  )


The exact form will vary between participants and between sessions; that variation is itself part of the lesson.
How different were the two outputs? Did the second version use column names that exist in the data? Did Copilot construct mass_change_g itself or did you have to prompt for it?

title: Block 2: AI - Inline completions
text:
Activity: Build a small analysis


Build a small analysis


Working on the same script you set up in the context demonstration, drive inline completion through a four-step analysis. Write the comment for each step first, then accept, reject, or modify the suggestion.
1. Filter to subjects with non-missing metabolic_rate_post and create a derived variable mass_change_g.
2. Produce a summary table of mean and standard deviation of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with sample sizes per cell.
3. Fit a linear model of metabolic_rate_post on treatment_arm and sex. Inspect the coefficients.
4. Produce one diagnostic plot relating mass_change_g to metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm.
For each step, your deliverable is the comment you wrote, the code Copilot suggested, and a one-line note on whether you accepted it, modified it, or rejected it and wrote something else. Recording this makes you notice when you accepted something without inspecting it.
Work in pairs. Each partner attempts steps 2 and 4 independently before comparing. Comparing usually shows variation: different suggestions, different acceptance decisions, and (often) different bugs.

title: Block 2: AI - Inline completions
text:
Check your understanding
The single most reliable way to improve the quality of inline completion suggestions in a new script is to:

Switch to a different underlying modelOpen more files in the editor as additional contextWrite a detailed comment immediately before the code you want, including data frame name and column namesRestart the IDE so Copilot has a fresh context

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Setup
AI is at its most useful for debugging code you wrote. You know what you intended; the AI can spot syntactic mistakes you missed, suggest fixes for runtime errors, and help you interpret unfamiliar error messages. The verification cost is low, because you are comparing the AI’s diagnosis against your own intention rather than against an unknown ground truth.
This block uses four error types, ordered by how much the debugger needs to know. The first error is a call to a function that does not exist, which Copilot can catch with no data; the second requires knowledge of the data values; the third requires knowledge of ggplot2’s grammar; the fourth runs cleanly, returns a plausible answer, and is wrong, so that only knowledge of the expected result reveals it. The differences matter, because they show where AI can substitute for documentation lookup, where it cannot substitute for inspecting the data, and where it cannot substitute for knowing the biology.
⏱ ~30 minutes
Have the voles dataset loaded:
library(tidyverse)
voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "voles_metabolism.csv"))

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 1: A missing function


Exercise 1: A missing function


You wrote the following to count voles per treatment:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_barchart()

R returns:
Error in geom_barchart() : could not find function "geom_barchart"
1. Paste both the code and the error message into your script as a block comment, then add # Fix this code: and let Copilot suggest a continuation:

# This code gives an error:
# ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
#   geom_barchart()
#
# Error in geom_barchart() : could not find function "geom_barchart"
#
# Fix this code:

Before accepting any suggestion, write a single sentence explaining why the original failed. Your sentence is the verification step. If you can write the sentence, you understood the fix; if you cannot, the AI has solved the problem but you have not learned anything.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_bar()

The function is geom_bar(), not geom_barchart(). ggplot2’s geom functions use short names; there is no _chart suffix anywhere in the package. The error message “could not find function” is the standard R response when a function does not exist in any loaded package, and it is the easiest class of error to recognise.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 2: A logic error


Exercise 2: A logic error


You wrote the following to filter to high-dose voles and compute mean post-treatment mass:

high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

The code runs without error and returns:
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_mass
      <dbl>
1       NaN
This is harder than the missing-function error, because there is no error message to paste. The code is doing exactly what you asked it to; the bug is in what you asked for. AI cannot diagnose this without first knowing what your data look like.
1. Before asking AI for help, inspect the data. Three diagnostic calls take seconds and tell you what you need to know:

voles |> distinct(treatment_arm)
voles |> count(treatment_arm)
nrow(high_dose)

The first two reveal that the values of treatment_arm (a character column, as read_csv() reads text by default) are Control, Low_dose, and High_dose (initial capital, underscore between words). The third returns zero. At this point you have already diagnosed the bug without involving an AI.
2. With the diagnostic information in hand, paste both the code and the diagnostic output into Chat (or as a block comment in your script) and ask for confirmation of the diagnosis:
# I am trying to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles. My code:

#  high_dose <- voles |>
#    filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

#  high_dose |>
#    summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

# returns NaN. But voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) returns
# "Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose". I think the filter is failing
# because of the case. Is that the only problem?
The exercise is to ask the question with the diagnostic context already in place, rather than asking AI to diagnose blind. AI is faster than you at typo-spotting and syntax recall, but slower than distinct() at telling you what is actually in your data.


Solution


high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "High_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g, na.rm = TRUE))

The capitalisation now matches the actual value in the data. Adding na.rm = TRUE is precautionary; for this dataset there are no missing values in mass_post_g, but in real biological data there usually are.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 3: An aesthetic-mapping error


Exercise 3: An aesthetic-mapping error


You wanted a scatter plot of post-treatment metabolic rate against post-treatment mass, coloured by treatment arm:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(color = treatment_arm) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

R returns:
Error: object 'treatment_arm' not found
1. Paste code and error as before, and ask Copilot for a fix. Before accepting, write a sentence on why R could not find treatment_arm, even though it is a column in voles.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = treatment_arm)) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

treatment_arm is a column in the data, so the mapping must go inside aes(). The color = argument outside aes() expects a fixed value such as "red" or "#0072B2", not a variable name. Because color = treatment_arm sits outside aes(), R evaluates it as an ordinary argument: it looks for an object called treatment_arm in your global environment, does not find one, and stops before ggplot2 ever looks inside the data. That is why the message names no function and does not mention the data at all. British spelling colour works as an alias for color in ggplot2.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
section: Exercise 4: A correct-looking but wrong result
text:
Exercise 4: A correct-looking but wrong result


Exercise 4: A correct-looking but wrong result


You want the mean change in body mass by treatment arm. You write:

voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

The code runs. There is no error and no NaN. It returns something like:
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  treatment_arm mean_change
  <chr>               <dbl>
1 Control             -0.21
2 Low_dose            -1.49
3 High_dose           -3.19
Every value is a small number of grams, which is entirely plausible for a vole, so nothing here looks wrong on its face. But the result is the reverse of the truth. The treatment was administered to increase body mass, and the dataset was built so that mass rises with dose. The table reports that mass falls, and falls most at the highest dose.
This is the error class that neither your diagnostics nor an AI can reliably catch for you. glimpse(), distinct(), and count() all report a clean dataset, because the data are clean; the fault is in the arithmetic, and the arithmetic produces a plausible number. The subtraction is the wrong way round. mass_pre_g - mass_post_g measures loss, when you wanted gain.






Note



A chat model will sometimes flag mass_pre_g - mass_post_g anyway, because “post minus pre” is the usual convention for a change score in its training data. That is pattern-matching on a convention, not a check of your result: the model cannot know which direction your treatment should push body mass unless you tell it, and plenty of valid analyses define change the other way round. Do not rely on it to catch this class of error.


1. Before you trust any result that runs cleanly, write down what a correct result should look like. For this table: the sign should be positive, because the treatment adds mass, and the magnitude should increase from Control to High_dose. Only then compare. The mismatch between “should be positive and increasing” and “is negative and decreasing” is the diagnosis.
2. You may give the code to AI for a second opinion, but it can only help if you supply the expected direction. A prompt that says “this should show increasing mass gain with dose, but it shows decreasing values; what is wrong?” will get the sign error named. A prompt that gives only the code and the output will get a description of what the code does, which is not the same as catching that it does the wrong thing.


Solution


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

mass_change_g is post minus pre, not pre minus post. With the subtraction the right way round the means are positive and increase with dose, matching the design of the study. The original ran without complaint because subtraction is defined in both directions; the only signal that it was wrong was knowing what the answer should be.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
The debugging checklist
When code fails, the order matters. Inspect the data first, ask the AI second.

Read the error message in full. The function name and the phrase (“could not find function”, “object not found”, “non-numeric argument”) usually localise the bug.
Inspect the relevant data. glimpse(), distinct() on character or factor columns, summary() on numeric columns, and nrow() after a filter are the four commands that catch most logic errors in seconds.
Verify variable names exactly, including capitalisation and underscores. Most “object not found” errors are typos.
If steps 1 to 3 do not localise the bug, paste the code, the error message, and the diagnostic output into Chat together. The combination is much more useful than the error alone.
After AI suggests a fix, write a one-sentence explanation of why the original failed. If you cannot write the sentence, you have not understood the fix.
Before trusting a result that runs without error, state in advance what it should look like: the sign, the rough magnitude, and the expected ordering. Compare the output against that statement. This is the one check AI cannot perform for you, because it requires knowing the biology.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Check your understanding
When a ggplot2 call stops with Error: object 'X' not found, and X is a column in your data, the most common cause is:

The data argument was supplied incorrectlyA column name was used outside aes() where ggplot2 expected a fixed valueThe ggplot2 package is not loadedThe variable contains missing values

title: Block 4: GitHub Copilot Chat in Ask mode
text:
What Chat sees, and what it does not
GitHub Copilot Chat comes with the same Copilot plan as inline completion, but it gives a different kind of help, and it does not necessarily use the same model: the chat model and the inline-completion model are configured separately. Inline completion is best when you are actively writing code and want quick suggestions or continuations. Chat is better for higher-level tasks such as planning an approach, understanding an error, or discussing design decisions. Chat requests need more computation, so they are the part of Copilot most likely to run into your plan’s usage limits (at the time of writing, October 2026, a monthly allowance of GitHub AI Credits). The two tools complement each other rather than replace one another.
⏱ ~30 minutes
Here GitHub Copilot Chat differs from a general chatbot such as ChatGPT, and the difference is easy to get wrong. A general chatbot sees what you paste or upload, plus whatever you have connected it to through its own connectors; it has no built-in link to your editor or your R session. GitHub Copilot is integrated with your repository and editor and can draw on context you did not paste. How much it draws on, and whether it can act on your machine, depends on where you use it. Three surfaces matter for this workshop, and they are not equivalent.
Separately from the surface, your repository’s .github/copilot-instructions.md, if present, is added automatically to Copilot Chat requests in that repository or workspace (see Block 6). Exactly what else is pulled in automatically has changed between versions and differs across surfaces, so the reliable habit is to set the context yourself (by pasting, attaching, or #-referencing) rather than to assume.
Run these exercises in Browser Chat, in Ask mode.
Browser Chat (all IDEs, including RStudio): navigate to your repository on github.com and click the Copilot icon in the top right. This is the one that works for everyone.
In-IDE Chat panel (VS Code and Positron): open the chat view, and use # references or Add Context to control what it sees. Both also offer slash commands: type / in the chat box to see the list for your editor. In VS Code these include /explain to describe what code does and /fix to propose a correction, which act on the code you have selected. Posit Assistant in Positron has its own set, such as /plan to draft a plan before changing code and /new to start a fresh conversation.
RStudio users should use the browser Chat throughout this block. RStudio’s own Posit Assistant chat is not part of your Copilot plan, so we do not use it here. Positron and VS Code users may use either browser or in-IDE chat; the exercises work in both, subject to the context caveat above.
crumbs: Block 4: GitHub Copilot Chat in Ask mode

title: Block 4: GitHub Copilot Chat in Ask mode
text:
Browser Chat on github.com: open your repository on github.com and select the Copilot icon. It works in the context of that repository and can reach its files, but it has no connection to your local machine, runs no code, and cannot see your R session. This is the one that behaves the same for everyone.
VS Code Chat panel: Copilot Chat is built into VS Code. It can see your open files, and you can add context explicitly: type # in the chat box to reference a file or #codebase for the whole workspace, or use the Add Context button. It does not see the objects in your R session unless you paste them, or unless an agent runs code for you.
Positron Chat panel: Positron’s built-in chat is now Posit Assistant, which replaced the deprecated Positron Assistant and is the default AI experience from Positron 2026.07. It is not Copilot Chat: it runs on a model provider you choose, either Posit’s own subscription or a bring-your-own provider such as GitHub Copilot. The difference that matters is the context it adds. Posit Assistant is given context about your interactive data science work, such as your loaded data, plots, and console history, and it can run code. So in Positron the “cannot see your data” assumption does not hold the way it does in browser Chat. See the Posit Assistant documentation.










Note



An assistant can describe your data confidently for two different reasons: (1) it has been given real information about your session, or (2) it is recalling something from training data. Only the first is reliable.
It has real information when one of these holds: you pasted the output (glimpse(), summary(), the printed result), or the data sits in a file it can read.
In Positron, Posit Assistant is given your session context, and it can run code and read the output.
It is guessing from training data when none of those apply, which is the case in browser Chat on github.com unless the data file is in the repository or you have pasted its structure. Tells: it substitutes a well-known dataset (mtcars, iris, penguins) you never mentioned, or asserts column names, factor levels, or values you never supplied.
Even when context is supplied, the model’s claim about what it can see is unreliable, and the context may be structure rather than actual values. Verify any data-specific claim against your real object.
crumbs: Block 4: GitHub Copilot Chat in Ask mode

title: Block 4: GitHub Copilot Chat in Ask mode
text:
Exercise 1: Reading a stack trace


Exercise 1: Reading a stack trace


This exercise shows how much the quality of Chat’s answers depends on the context you supply.
If you use in-IDE chat in Positron, start from a session without voles loaded (or use browser Chat), so that the session context does not hand over the answer.
1. Open a fresh Chat session. Paste only the following error message and ask “What does this error mean?”:
Error in `mutate()`:
ℹ In argument: `mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g`.
Caused by error:
! object 'mass_post' not found
Read the answer. It will be reasoning from the error alone.
Try changing the model in the model picker below the prompt box, if your plan allows it, and compare the answers. (At the time of writing, Copilot Free and Copilot Student offer only Auto, where Copilot chooses the model for you.)
2. Now open a new Chat session and paste the same error along with the code that produced it and the output of glimpse(voles):
I am running this code:

  voles |>
    mutate(mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g)

and getting:

  Error in `mutate()`:
  ℹ In argument: `mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g`.
  Caused by error:
  ! object 'mass_post' not found

The data structure is:

  Rows: 72
  Columns: 6
  $ subject_id          <chr> "V001", "V002", "V003", ...
  $ sex                 <chr> "M", "F", "M", ...
  $ treatment_arm       <chr> "Control", "Control", ...
  $ mass_pre_g          <dbl> 28.3, 27.9, 30.1, ...
  $ mass_post_g         <dbl> 28.5, 28.0, 30.5, ...
  $ metabolic_rate_post <dbl> 13.21, 12.84, 13.55, ...

What is wrong?
Read this answer. It will name the specific bug (a missing _g suffix on mass_post) and propose the fix.
3. Now open a new Chat session, attach the file from the repository, and try pasting the error message:








With the file itself in context, Copilot can see the column names directly, so it should again identify the missing _g suffix, this time without your having pasted glimpse() output. No one route is the correct one. The answer is only as good as the context, and context reaches the model by more than one route: what you paste, and what the surface can already read.
Compare the three answers. The first reasons from the error text alone and can only guess. The second and third both locate the specific bug, because both were given the column names, one by your paste and one by reading the file.

title: Block 4: GitHub Copilot Chat in Ask mode
section: How much of your data to show
text:
How much of your data to show
The contents of your data can reach the model by three routes, and each is a disclosure:

You paste it into the chat: an error, an output, a printed result.
It reads a data file that sits in a repository or workspace it can see. Browser Chat on github.com works in the context of the repository you open it from, so a committed voles_metabolism.csv is within reach; in VS Code, Copilot can search your workspace when you use #codebase.
The IDE injects your session context. In Positron, Posit Assistant is given context about your interactive data science work, such as your loaded data, plots, and console history, so a data frame already in memory can reach it without a paste.

Describing your data to Chat is a recurring task, but pasting is not the only way your data is exposed. Before you decide what to show, know what the surface can already reach: a data file committed to the repo, or a tibble loaded in a Positron session, may have been disclosed already.
When you do describe a data frame deliberately, three commands reveal increasing amounts:

names(voles), or equivalently colnames(voles), lists the column names only, in their original order, and discloses nothing about the values. Prefer this to ls(voles), which returns the same names but sorts them alphabetically and so loses the column order.
summary(voles) adds the range, quartiles, and missing-value counts for numeric columns, and is less informative for character or factor columns. It reveals the shape of the data, not individual records.
glimpse(voles) and str(voles) add the first few actual values of every column.
crumbs: Block 4: GitHub Copilot Chat in Ask mode

title: Block 4: GitHub Copilot Chat in Ask mode
text:
Exercise 2: Refining an approach question


Exercise 2: Refining an approach question


Run this in browser Chat, or with no analysis file referenced. If your script is open in the editor, Copilot may infer the design from it, and the first answer will be less generic than described below. The refinement in step 2 still helps in that case, because your scientific question and your design intent are not written in any file; they exist only in your head until you state them.
1. Open a Chat session and ask, exactly as written:
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
Read the answer. With no design and no scientific question supplied, it will be a tour of paired t-tests, mixed models, change scores, ANCOVA, and so on, because the question is too vague to permit a recommendation.
2. In a new chat session, refine the question, with the dataset structure and the scientific question explicit:
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My biological question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass
relative to control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes
alongside any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible
primary analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
3. In a new chat session, add the raw data file as context.
Try asking the first, vague question again:
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
Compare all three answers. Which was best?
Even though the question is the same vague one from step 1, the file in context supplies the design that the prompt omits: column names, types, and the treatment arms. The answer should narrow accordingly, closer to step 2 than to step 1, without your having stated the design in prose.

When to use Chat versus inline
A short decision rule covers most cases:


Task

Yes

Marginal

No

No

The rule is not strict; the two tools overlap considerably. The principle is: inline for typing, Chat for thinking.

Check your understanding
Which statement best describes the context available to Copilot Chat in Ask mode, in the browser on github.com or in your IDE?

It sees only the text you paste into the prompt, nothing elseBeyond what you paste, it can draw on the repository or project it is opened from and on files you attach or reference; what else it sees (open files, your R session) depends on the surfaceIt has full automatic access to every file in the repository and to your running R session, on every surfaceIt can always execute your R code to read the data directly

title: Block 5: From Chat to Agent
text:
Three surfaces, before we start
In Block 4 you used Chat in Ask mode: you asked a question, it answered, and nothing on your machine or in your repository changed unless you copied the answer out yourself. This block introduces the shift that the rest of the workshop depends on, from an assistant that advises to an agent that acts. The configuration files you write in Block 6 exist because of this shift, so it is worth being precise about what changes, where it changes, and why it matters.
⏱ ~30 minutes
This workshop puts the same ideas in front of you through three different tools, and they do not all offer the same modes or honour the same files. You met this distinction in Block 4 for context; it returns here for actions, and it is the single thing most likely to make an exercise behave differently for the person next to you. Hold the three apart from the outset.
The blunt version: the cloud agent lives on github.com and is the same for everyone; Copilot in VS Code is the Copilot-aligned local agent; Posit Assistant is a separate local agent with its own configuration discovery. The one file both local agents read is AGENTS.md, which Block 6 returns to. Where a step depends on which tool you are using, it says so.

title: Block 5: From Chat to Agent
text:
Web-based GitHub Chat on github.com. It works in the context of the repository you open it from and can read its committed files, but it has no connection to your machine and runs no local code. Its agent is the Copilot cloud agent, which acts on the remote, on its own branch. This is the surface that behaves the same for everyone, which is why several exercises specify it.
GitHub Copilot Chat in VS Code. The in-editor Copilot. It reads Copilot’s instruction files (.github/copilot-instructions.md, and also an AGENTS.md in the repository), runs in your local session and, in Agent mode, acts on your files.
Posit Assistant. Posit’s assistant for Positron and RStudio. At the time of writing (October 2026) it ships as Positron’s default AI experience, replacing the now-deprecated Positron Assistant and Databot, and is also available in recent RStudio releases. You can use it through Posit’s managed Posit AI Pass subscription or with your own provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, and others; in Positron, GitHub Copilot is available as a provider in preview). It acts locally, like the VS Code agent, but it looks for configuration in its own places: it reads an AGENTS.md file in the project root, not Copilot’s .github/copilot-instructions.md, and it loads skills from .agents/skills/ (or its own .posit/assistant/skills/). That difference is the subject of Block 6 rather than this one.

title: Block 5: From Chat to Agent
text:
Ask, Plan, Agent
Beneath the surface differences, chat assistants offer more than one mode, and they differ in what the assistant is permitted to do, not in how clever it is. At the time of writing, Copilot Chat in VS Code offers Ask, Plan and Agent; Posit Assistant offers the same three ideas (an Ask mode, a /plan command, and its default agent behaviour). VS Code also used to offer an Edit mode that changed only the files you named; it was deprecated in VS Code 1.126 (June 2026), and that kind of change is now made in Agent mode. If you see Edit mode in an older tutorial, read it as “Agent mode restricted to named files”.

Ask mode answers in prose. It can read context and write code into the reply, but it changes nothing for you. Everything it suggests, you apply by hand. This is the mode you used throughout Block 4, and it is available on every surface, including web-based GitHub Chat.
Plan mode researches the task and returns a step-by-step plan: which files it would touch, in what order, and how it would check the result. It does not change your code while it plans; you review and amend the plan, and only when you approve it does the work begin. (In Posit Assistant, the plan is written to a Markdown plan file, which is the one file it writes while planning.)
Agent mode is given a goal rather than a file list. It decides which files to read, which to change, and what commands to run to reach the goal, then carries those steps out, often in a loop: make a change, run something, read the result, change again.

Agent mode runs in two distinct places, and the difference is where the changes land:

The in-IDE agent (Copilot in VS Code, or Posit Assistant in Positron or RStudio) works on the files on your own machine and runs commands in your local session, so its actions appear in your working directory in real time.
The cloud agent on github.com works on your repository on the remote, in an environment you do not see, and delivers its work on a branch, usually as a pull request you review and merge.

The progression is one of widening autonomy: Ask tells you, Plan tells you exactly what it intends to do and waits, Agent decides what to change and does it. A short way to hold the distinction is that in Ask mode you are the hands and the agent is the advisor; in Agent mode the agent is both.











Mode
Reads context
Writes code
Edits your files
Runs commands
Decides scope
Where it runs



Ask
Yes
Into the reply only
No
No
No
Any surface, incl. web


Plan
Yes
Into the plan only
No, until you approve
No, until you approve
Proposes it for your approval
In-IDE


Agent
Yes
Yes
Any it judges relevant
Yes
Yes
In-IDE or cloud agent









ImportantWhich modes you can actually run



These modes are not equally available on every plan, and the cloud agent in particular is gated. Plan names, allowances and billing change often; what follows is the position at the time of writing (October 2026), so check GitHub’s Copilot plans page for your own access before the course.

In-IDE Chat (Ask, Plan and Agent) is usable on Copilot Free, subject to a monthly allowance and to automatic model selection only (you cannot pick the model). Copilot Student, free to verified students, has the same Auto-only model choice. Paid plans draw on a monthly allowance of AI Credits and let you choose models. For this workshop the free allowance is enough to follow the exercises, though a heavy session can reach it; if your requests stop being answered, a limit rather than a bug is the likely cause. Posit Assistant’s limits depend on how you connect it: your Posit AI Pass, or the provider whose key you give it.
The Copilot cloud agent on github.com is not part of Copilot Free. It is included in Copilot Student, Pro, Pro+ and Max; on Copilot Business or Enterprise it depends on your organisation’s policy. Note that this is a Copilot plan, not a GitHub Pro account, which is a different product. If you are on Copilot Free, you can run agent mode inside your IDE but not the cloud agent on the website.

The practical consequence for the exercise below: everyone can run the in-IDE route, and the cloud-agent route on github.com is only open to those with a Copilot plan that includes it. The exercise is written so the in-IDE route is the default and the cloud agent is the variant, not the reverse.

title: Block 5: From Chat to Agent
section: Why this is the moment configuration starts to matter
text:
Why this is the moment configuration starts to matter
In Ask mode, a vague or unconventional answer costs you a re-read and a re-prompt. You are the filter: nothing reaches your files except what you choose to paste. An agent removes that filter. When the assistant edits files and runs commands on a goal you stated once, every convention it does not know, it will guess, and every guess lands in your project rather than in a reply you can ignore.
This is the practical reason the persistent-context mechanisms in Block 6 exist. A copilot-instructions.md (or AGENTS.md) that says you use the native pipe and write outputs only to a dedicated directory is mildly useful to an advisor and essential for an agent, because the agent acts on those conventions unsupervised. The looser the leash, the more the standing instructions matter. Put plainly: in Ask mode you can afford to correct the assistant after the fact; in Agent mode you want the conventions in place before it starts, because “after the fact” now means after your files have changed.
This is also where the three surfaces stop being interchangeable. A .github/copilot-instructions.md is honoured by web-based GitHub and by Copilot in VS Code, but Posit Assistant will not read it; Posit Assistant reads AGENTS.md instead, which Copilot also reads. An agent that cannot see your conventions does not become cautious; it proceeds anyway, on assumptions. So the surface you run the agent on decides whether the standing instructions you wrote are even in force, which is a reason to know which tool you are in before you hand it a goal.






Warning



Autonomy and trust are not the same thing. An agent that can run commands can run a wrong command. In the in-IDE agent that command executes in your local session as it works; on the cloud agent it executes in the remote environment before its work reaches you. Either way it acts before you have read it. Two habits limit the damage, and both are reasons the Block 6 instructions file matters: forbid destructive operations in standing instructions (no rm(list = ls()), no overwriting raw data, outputs only to dedicated directories), and keep the agent working against version control so any change it makes is a diff you can inspect and revert. Never run an agent with uncommitted work you are not prepared to lose.

title: Block 5: From Chat to Agent
section: Exercise: the same task, three modes
text:
Exercise: the same task, three modes


The same task, three modes


This exercise makes the difference concrete by giving the same kind of task to each mode in turn, growing the scope as the autonomy grows. Steps 1 and 2 use a deliberately small change so the mode, not the task, is what you are watching; step 3 hands the agent a larger, end-to-end job that a single edit could not cover, because that is the kind of job an agent is for. Have your forked workshop repository to hand, committed and clean, so that anything the agent changes is a diff you can inspect.
1. Ask mode. This works on any surface. In Ask mode, prompt:
In scripts/01_load_data.R, I want to add a column mass_change that is
mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g. How do I do that?
Read the answer. It will tell you the line to add and roughly where, and possibly explain the mutate() call. Notice what has not happened: the file is unchanged. To apply this you would copy the line into the script yourself.
2. Plan mode. This is a local-IDE step; if you are on web-based GitHub, read it and move on. In Copilot Chat in VS Code, switch to Plan mode (in Posit Assistant, type /plan), and give the same instruction as an instruction rather than a question:
Add a column mass_change that is mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g to
scripts/01_load_data.R. Change no other file.
Now you are offered a plan, not a change: which file it will edit, where, and how it will check the result. Read it before approving. Nothing has changed yet; the decision to go ahead is still yours, and you can narrow or correct the plan first. When you approve, it carries the plan out and you see the diff against that one file.
3. Agent mode. Now the task grows beyond a single edit. Rather than name a change, you state an outcome that spans the pipeline: a new derived variable, a plot that uses it, and the surrounding work needed to keep everything running. This is the kind of job that distinguishes an agent from an editor, because no one file is named and the agent must read the project, decide what to touch, and verify its own work.
This step has two routes. Use the in-IDE route if you are in Copilot in VS Code or Posit Assistant; use the cloud-agent route only if your Copilot plan includes the cloud agent (see the availability note above). The goal is the same for both; what differs is where the work happens and how it comes back to you.
In-IDE agent (default route). Switch the Chat panel to Agent mode and give it the goal:
In the voles pipeline, read data/voles_metabolism.csv through the existing
loading step, add a derived mass_change column (mass_post_g minus
mass_pre_g), and create a new script that produces an exploratory plot of
mass_change by treatment_arm. Make sure the loading step and the rest of
the pipeline still run end to end.
Watch what it does in your working directory. It cannot satisfy this from one edit: it must locate the loading step, decide whether the derived column belongs there or in a new script, write the plotting code in a new file, and run the pipeline to confirm nothing downstream broke. It works in a loop, editing then running then reading the result, and you see each change land in your working tree as it goes. This is why you committed first: every file the agent writes or alters is a diff you can inspect, accept, or revert. Read the diff before you keep it; the agent’s confidence that the pipeline “still runs” is its claim, and a claim is not a check until you have seen the output yourself.
Cloud agent route. On github.com, hand the same goal to the Copilot cloud agent. The mechanics are worth seeing once, because a pull request is how an agent’s work reaches a real project.

Open the Agents panel on github.com (or start from Copilot Chat on your repository), choose your fork, and give it the same goal as above. There is no separate “agent mode” switch on github.com: starting a task from the Agents panel is handing it to the cloud agent. You can also assign a GitHub Issue to Copilot, but for this exercise prompting it directly is enough.
The agent starts a session on the remote, in an environment you do not see. It works on a new branch rather than your default branch, so nothing it does affects your main line of work until you decide it should.
It then works through the goal on that branch, committing as it goes: reading the data, editing the loading step, adding the plotting script, and running the pipeline to check it. You can follow its progress in the session log while it runs, and steer or stop it from the Agents page if it heads the wrong way.
When it finishes, you can review its changes and ask for refinements before anything is proposed for merging; ask it for a pull request (or include “open a pull request” in your first prompt). A pull request is a proposed merge: a named, reviewable bundle of commits asking to be brought into your main branch. This is the unit you review, not the individual edits.
Open the pull request and read the Files changed tab. This is the diff: every line the agent added or removed, across every file it touched. Read it as you would a colleague’s contribution, because that is what it is. Check that the derived column is computed correctly, that the plot uses the right variables, and that nothing unrelated was changed.
If you are satisfied, merge the pull request, which brings the changes into your main branch on the remote; then git pull locally to bring them to your machine. If you are not satisfied, you can comment on the pull request to ask the agent to revise it, or simply close it and discard the branch. Nothing reaches your main branch, or your local working tree, until you choose to merge.

The review step is built into the cloud agent’s flow: it never edits your working files directly, and its work arrives on a branch as a proposal you approve rather than a change you discover. The in-IDE agent gives you speed and immediacy; the cloud agent gives you a review gate by default.
Whichever route you took, notice the autonomy you handed over: you specified an outcome and the agent chose the steps, the files, and the order. The agent decides just as much on both routes. What differs is where its decisions take effect: live in your working tree, or on a branch behind a pull request you approve first.
4. The point of the comparison. Re-read the results together. What differed across the modes was how much you decided versus how much the assistant decided. In Ask mode you placed every character. In Plan mode you approved a stated intention, for one file you named, before anything changed. In Agent mode you approved an outcome and trusted the agent to choose the files, the steps, and the order, whether that ran live in your working tree or on a branch behind a pull request. The step-3 task was large enough that you could not have specified it edit by edit in advance, which is the point: an agent is for the jobs where stating the goal is tractable but stating every step is not. Ask yourself whether the agent structured the pipeline the way you would have, whether the plot answers the question you meant, and whether you would have caught it had it not. That question, scaled up to a task you cannot read line by line, is why the standing instructions in Block 6 are written before the agent runs, not after, and why it matters that the surface you run on is one that reads them.

title: Block 5: From Chat to Agent
text:
Check your understanding
What is the key difference between Ask mode and Agent mode in GitHub Copilot?

Agent mode uses a more capable underlying model than Ask modeAsk mode answers without changing anything, whereas Agent mode can decide which files to change and which commands to run, and carries those actions outAsk mode is free and Agent mode is always paidAgent mode can only be used on github.com, never in an IDE

Where does the in-IDE agent apply its changes, compared with the cloud agent on github.com?

Both apply changes only as a pull request you review before mergingThe in-IDE agent edits the files in your local working directory in real time, whereas the cloud agent works on a branch on the remote and returns its work for review, usually as a pull requestBoth edit your local files directly with no review stepThe in-IDE agent cannot run commands, only the cloud agent can

Why do persistent instruction files matter more once you are using an agent than when you are using Ask mode?

Agents cannot read pasted context, so the file is the only way to inform themAn agent acts on its assumptions by editing files and running commands unsupervised, so conventions it does not know are applied to your project rather than merely appearing in a reply you can discardInstruction files are required for Agent mode to function at allAsk mode ignores instruction files entirely

title: Block 6: Custom instructions and skills
text:
Before you start: which assistant are you actually using?
Block 5 argued that an agent acts on conventions it cannot see, and that the looser the leash, the more those standing conventions matter. This block shows how to make those conventions visible to the assistant in advance, so you do not restate them in every comment and every Chat session. It falls into two parts. Part A covers the always-on mechanisms, custom instructions and scoped instructions, which load automatically and behave the same for everyone on a surface that reads them; you will test these mostly in Ask mode, the mode from Block 5 where you remain the filter. Part B moves to agent mode and to skills, which are invoked rather than always loaded and are far more surface-dependent. It also returns to Plan mode as the review step that sits between asking and handing a goal to a fully autonomous agent.
⏱ ~60 minutes

title: Block 6: Custom instructions and skills
text:
Warning





You met Copilot in VS Code and Posit Assistant in Block 5. This is the detail that matters now that you are writing configuration files, because the two read those files from different places, and confusing them is the single most common reason a configuration file appears to be ignored. (If you used Positron Assistant on an earlier course or in an older Positron, note that it is now deprecated: since Positron 2026.07, Posit Assistant is Positron’s default AI experience.)
GitHub Copilot (on github.com, in the cloud agent, and in VS Code) reads .github/copilot-instructions.md, scoped .github/instructions/*.instructions.md files, and AGENTS.md. It loads skills from .github/skills/, .claude/skills/ or .agents/skills/.
Posit Assistant, in Positron and RStudio, reads AGENTS.md in the project root as its project instructions; it does not read .github/copilot-instructions.md. It loads skills automatically when they are relevant, from .agents/skills/ or its own .posit/assistant/skills/ (older versions used .positai/; extra locations can be set with skills.paths). It does not look in .github/skills/.
The blunt rule of thumb, at the time of writing (October 2026): the files both tools read are AGENTS.md for instructions and .agents/skills/ for skills. This block teaches Copilot’s .github/ files because they are what the cloud agent and code review on github.com use, and because scoped instructions have no Posit Assistant equivalent; if you work in Posit Assistant, put your always-on instructions in AGENTS.md and your skills in .agents/skills/. Where this block depends on behaviour that differs between the two tools it says so, because both are moving targets and guessing wastes your time.

title: Block 6: Custom instructions and skills
text:
Part A: Instructions and scoping
The two mechanisms in this part share one property that makes them dependable: they load automatically, without your asking. You do not invoke them, you do not name them, and you do not have to remember they exist. They are also the right place to start, because everything you learn here works the same for everyone on a surface that reads the file in question, with less of the surface-dependence that complicates Part B.
Providing context to models
GitHub Copilot, like any LLM client, provides several ways to supply context, distinguished by how they load.
Workspace-level custom instructions live in .github/copilot-instructions.md. Copilot loads this file automatically for every request: in web-based GitHub Chat, the cloud agent, code review, and Copilot Chat in VS Code. (Posit Assistant does not read it, per the orientation above.) Use it for things that are always true of your project: which packages you use, your naming conventions, your file structure, your statistical conventions. The file should be short and broad in scope; treat two pages as a ceiling, not a target.
Scoped instructions live in .github/instructions/*.instructions.md, with a YAML front-matter applyTo glob that restricts the file to particular paths (for example applyTo: "**/*.qmd" to apply only to Quarto documents). Use them for rules that apply to one kind of file but not the rest. They load automatically when Copilot works on a matching file, and are used alongside copilot-instructions.md, not instead of it. Support differs by surface: in VS Code, Copilot Chat honours applyTo and attaches the file when the agent works on a matching file; on GitHub.com, at the time of writing, scoped instructions are used only by the cloud agent and by Copilot code review. Posit Assistant has no equivalent. If your work is mainly in one tool, confirm it supports the mechanism before relying on it.
Agent instructions live in an AGENTS.md file, usually in the repository root. AGENTS.md is a cross-tool convention rather than a Copilot one: Copilot reads it (and gives precedence to the nearest AGENTS.md in the directory tree), and it is the file Posit Assistant reads for project instructions. If your group uses more than one assistant, it is the most portable place for always-on conventions.
Agent Skills live in .github/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md (or .agents/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md, which Posit Assistant also reads), with a YAML front-matter name and description. Unlike the mechanisms above, skills are not always loaded; they are invoked. Either you type /skill-name, or the assistant infers from the description that the skill is relevant. Skills are the subject of Part B; they are listed here only to complete the picture.
A further, related mechanism is custom prompt files (.github/prompts/*.prompt.md), invoked explicitly as slash commands. These are outside the scope of this workshop.
The mechanisms answer different questions. Custom instructions (and AGENTS.md) answer “how should code in this project be written?” Scoped instructions answer “how should this kind of file be written?” Skills answer “how should this specific task be executed?”
How to write effective instructions
A copilot-instructions.md file is loaded into every interaction on a reading surface, and is read by the cloud agent before it starts work, so its length is a recurring cost. A handful of accurate lines outperforms a long file.
A few principles carry most of the value:

Write each instruction as a single, simple statement. If you have several points, use several lines rather than one dense paragraph; the model parses discrete statements more reliably than prose.
Describe the conventions you actually follow, not the ones you aspire to. An instruction your own code routinely breaks teaches the model a rule the surrounding code contradicts, which makes its suggestions less consistent.
Be concrete and positive. “Use the native pipe |>” and “snake_case for all object names” are actionable; “write clean, idiomatic code” is not.
Avoid contradiction and overlap. When a file matches a scoped instruction, Copilot is given both that file and copilot-instructions.md; GitHub documents no rule for which wins when they disagree, so do not rely on one quietly overriding the other.

More set-up advice and principles are in the GitHub documentation on onboarding an instruction file.


Example

# Copilot Instructions: R Analytical Repository

This repository contains analytical R code for computationally reproducible
research. Most items below are written for you to follow as you generate code.
A short Verification section lists the few things that are also checked in CI,
because a silent failure there is costly.

## Canary
Start any response that writes or edits R code with this as the first line of
the first code block:
`# copilot-instructions: active v4`

## Priorities
When two instructions conflict and no test settles it, prefer in this order:
correctness, reproducibility, transparency, interpretability, maintainability.
Note the trade-off in the pull request description.

## Agent behaviour
Never wait for human input in committed code. Do not use `readline()`,
`menu()`, `file.choose()`, `browser()`, or `View()`. When an input is missing,
add a `# DEFAULT:` comment naming the assumption and the value you chose, then
carry on.

## Naming and style
- Use the native pipe `|>`, not `%>%`.
- Use snake_case for all objects and functions.
- Assign with `<-`, not `=`.
- Write `TRUE` and `FALSE`, never `T` and `F`.
- Suffix dataframe and tibble objects with `_df`; raw import objects use `_raw`
  instead and are never reassigned.
- Suffix fitted models with `_model`.
- Suffix ggplot objects with `_plot`.
- Namespace-qualify calls (`pkg::fun()`) inside `R/functions/`. In analysis
  scripts, load packages with `library()` at the top and use bare names below.
- Avoid hidden global state and partial argument matching.
- Abstract logic into a function once it appears in three or more places.

## Reproducibility
- Never use `setwd()` or `rm(list = ls())`.
- Build every path with `here::here()`; relative paths only.
- Assume each script runs from a fresh R session.
- Manage dependencies with `renv`.
- Set a seed before any stochastic operation.
- Save `sessioninfo::session_info()` to the output directory at the end of each
  top-level script.

## Dependencies (renv)
- Manage all dependencies with `renv`; the project library is the only source
  of truth.
- Never call `install.packages()`. Add a package with `renv::install()`, then
  `renv::snapshot(prompt = FALSE)`.
- When `renv.lock` already lists the packages you need, restore rather than
  install: `renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)`.
- Never edit `renv.lock` by hand.
- Set `options(renv.config.auto.snapshot = FALSE)` so the lockfile is never
  written as a side effect; snapshot only deliberately.
- Use `renv::snapshot(type = "all")` so the lockfile is reproducible across
  runs rather than depending on usage detection.

## Reading and writing data
- Always use functions from readr (`readr::read_*(col_types = ...)`), not
  `read.*`.
- Keep raw data files immutable; never overwrite anything in the raw data
  directory.
- Separate raw data, derived data, scripts, outputs, and documentation.
- Write outputs only to dedicated output directories, never outside the
  repository.
- Assign cleaned and derived results to new objects; do not overwrite the raw
  import object.

## Data integrity
- Never drop missing data silently. Filter with a stated reason, or use
  `tidyr::drop_na()` on named columns.
- Prefer `purrr::map_*()` and `vapply()` over `sapply()`.

## Statistical practice
- Distinguish exploratory from confirmatory analyses, in prose or chunk labels.
- Validate model assumptions with `performance::check_model()` for regression
  models and record the inspection.

## Figures
For any figure, quick or polished:
- Use tidyverse style, the native pipe, and British spelling.
- Build paths with `here::here()`.
- No pie charts, dual y-axes, 3D effects, or dynamite plots (bar plus error
  bar) when raw data exist.
- Never use `theme_grey()`; default to `theme_minimal()` or `theme_classic()`.
- For categorical groups, add `shape` or `linetype` alongside colour.
- Use `linewidth`, not `size`, for line and density layers.
- For figures meant for an audience, follow the pub-figures skill in full.

## Code chunks
- Keep chunks short: one logical step each (import, clean, transform, model,
  diagnose, or visualise), and no more than about 40 lines.
- Comment the rationale for the step, not the mechanics of each line.
- Include at least one comment per chunk.

## Quarto
For `.qmd` files: render from a clean session, give chunks informative labels,
and avoid hidden dependencies between chunks.

## Verification (also checked in CI)
These are enforced because a silent miss is costly:
- No `setwd(`, `%>%`, `install.packages(`, or absolute paths in committed code.
- `renv::status()` reports a synchronised library.
- Each script and `.qmd` runs or renders in a fresh `--vanilla` session without
  error.
- The raw data directory is unchanged by any run.
- Outputs resolve inside the repository.

## Specialist instructions and skills
Specialised instruction files hold domain standards and repository policy;
skills hold procedural workflows. When one applies, follow it alongside these
instructions. Skill selection follows each skill's own description.

Activity: Build your copilot-instructions.md file


Build your copilot-instructions.md file


In the workshop template repository (which you forked at the start of the day), you will create .github/copilot-instructions.md. Rather than start from a blank file, generate a skeleton and then refine it. The refining is the real exercise.
Step 1: Before and after. This is a controlled before-and-after: the same prompt, run twice in the same mode, with the instructions file the only thing that changes between the runs. Unlike the Block 5 exercise, where the mode changed between runs, here the mode is held fixed (Ask) and the file is the single variable.
Run the prompt, in Ask mode, with no instructions file present:
Read in data/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot of
mass_post_g by treatment arm.

You can do this in your IDE’s chat or by heading to the repository on GitHub.

Keep this answer. It is your baseline.
Step 2: Draft a skeleton.
If you have an in-IDE agent (Copilot in VS Code, or Posit Assistant in Positron or RStudio): open the chat in Agent mode and prompt, “Create .github/copilot-instructions.md by reading the current workspace.” The assistant reads the repository and drafts a file covering the structure, languages, and packages it detects. If Posit Assistant is your main tool, ask for AGENTS.md in the project root instead, because that is the file it reads (Copilot reads AGENTS.md too); everywhere this activity says copilot-instructions.md, read AGENTS.md.
If you have no in-IDE agent: create .github/copilot-instructions.md by hand. Either take the example above, or, if it is easier, push an empty file and use GitHub.com’s web Chat to generate a draft once it is on the remote. Hand-authoring is fine; the file is short.
Step 3: Trim it hard. Generated instructions run long and generic. Cut the draft down to what is always true of the project and broadly useful, treating two pages as a ceiling, not a target. Delete anything the model padded or guessed at.
Step 4: Make it yours. The generator reads the workshop template, not your own work, and it cannot read your judgement. Edit the file so that it specifies, at minimum:

One naming or style convention you actually hold that the generator did not infer: the native pipe over %>%, <- over =, a suffix scheme for objects, whichever you genuinely follow. The test is whether your own existing code obeys it.
One project-structure fact the model cannot guess from a fresh template: where raw data live and that they are immutable, where outputs are written, where functions are sourced from. State it as a single declarative line.
One statistical or reproducibility convention that is always true of your work: that paths are built with here::here(), that a seed is set before any stochastic step, that exploratory and confirmatory analyses are labelled as such.
A canary line you can verify. Instruct Copilot to begin any response that writes R code with a fixed first comment, for example # copilot-instructions: active. This is the cheapest possible test of whether the file is being read at all: if the canary is absent, the file is not loading, and you are debugging the wrong thing.

Keep each as a single, simple statement. Four accurate lines you can verify are worth more than two pages of generated prose you cannot.
Step 5: Commit and push. Commit .github/copilot-instructions.md and push to your fork on GitHub. This is what makes the file available where it is read most reliably, and it is the point at which users of every IDE converge: from here on, everyone works the same way.
Step 6: Verify. Open a fresh chat session, on GitHub.com or in your IDE, and run the same prompt as Step 1:
Read in data/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot of
mass_post_g by treatment arm.
Read the answer against your Step 1 baseline. If your canary line appears, the file is loading. If the plot follows the conventions you wrote in Step 4, in particular the one only you could have supplied, the instructions are doing their job. If the canary is missing, the file is not being found: check that it sits at exactly .github/copilot-instructions.md (or AGENTS.md in the project root), that it is committed and pushed, and that instruction files are enabled in your settings.


Compare your answer with what someone else gets from their own instructions file. The differences reflect your different standards.
Activity: Write a scoped instruction for Quarto documents
A scoped instruction is a file of rules that applies only to certain files in your project. It lives in .github/instructions/ and carries an applyTo glob in its front matter that names the paths it covers, for example applyTo: "**/*.qmd" to apply only to Quarto documents. When Copilot works on a file that matches the glob, the rules load automatically; when it works on any other file, they do not.






NoteWhen to use a scoped file



The test for whether something belongs in a scoped file rather than the always-on copilot-instructions.md is simple: would the rule be wrong, not merely irrelevant, in the files the glob excludes? If a rule is true everywhere (use the native pipe, use snake_case), it belongs in the always-on file; putting it in a scoped file gains nothing and adds the scoped mechanism’s reliability problems. A rule earns a scoped file only when it is a property of one file type and would mislead the model elsewhere.


Quarto .qmd files are a clear case for an R user, because they carry concerns a plain .R script does not have at all: chunk options, how code is echoed into the rendered document, figure captions and dimensions, and a working-directory trap specific to rendering. An instruction to set echo: false is correct inside a .qmd and meaningless inside scripts/02_analysis.R.


Create a scoped instruction file


Create .github/instructions/quarto.instructions.md with the following content:
---
applyTo: "**/*.qmd"
---

# Quarto document conventions

These rules apply to Quarto source files only. They concern how code is
presented and rendered in the document, not the analysis logic itself.

## Chunk options
- Set chunk options with the hashpipe (`#|`) inside the chunk, not in the
  `{r}` header. For example `#| echo: false`, not `{r, echo=FALSE}`.
- Give every code chunk a label (`#| label: fig-mass-by-arm`) so cross-
  references and cached results are stable.
- Every chunk that produces a figure must set `#| fig-cap:` with a caption;
  do not emit an uncaptioned figure into a rendered document.

## Echo and output for a written report
- Default to `#| echo: false` so the rendered document shows results, not
  source, unless the document is explicitly a code walkthrough.
- Use `#| warning: false` and `#| message: false` on chunks that load
  packages or fit models, so loading noise does not appear in the output.

## Figures
- Label figure chunks with a `fig-` prefix and reference them in prose with
  `@fig-...`, not by a hardcoded number.
- Set figure dimensions explicitly with `#| fig-width:` and `#| fig-height:`
  rather than relying on defaults.

## Reproducibility
- Resolve paths with `here::here()` inside chunks; never assume the working
  directory is the document's folder, because Quarto and the R session may
  differ on this.
Test it. With the scoped file committed, open a .qmd file and, in Agent mode, ask Copilot to add a code chunk to that file (and change nothing else) that reads the voles data and plots mass_post_g by treatment_arm. A correct response uses hashpipe chunk options, labels the chunk with a fig- prefix, sets a fig-cap:, and resolves the path with here::here(). Then open a plain .R script and ask for the same plot in that file: the hashpipe and caption rules should not appear, because the scoped file does not apply there. That contrast, the same request producing different output in the two file types, is the demonstration. Run this test in Copilot in VS Code or with the cloud agent; Posit Assistant has no scoped-instruction mechanism.


Part A ends here. Everything so far has loaded automatically and, apart from one tightly scoped request, left you as the filter on what reaches your files. Part B removes that filter.

title: Block 6: Custom instructions and skills
section: Part B: Agent mode, Plan mode, and skills
text:
Part B: Agent mode, Plan mode, and skills
Part A’s mechanisms loaded whether or not you thought about them. Skills are different: they are invoked, not always loaded, and they live in an agent’s world, where the assistant acts rather than advises. Before the skill itself, it is worth returning to the mode that puts a review step in front of an agent.
Plan mode: the review step before action
Block 5 set out three modes: Ask, which answers; Plan, which proposes; and Agent, which decides scope and acts. You used Plan mode there on a one-line change, where it hardly earns its keep. Its value shows on a multi-step job.
Plan mode does not change your code while it plans. Given a goal, it produces an ordered, step-by-step plan of what it would do, which files it would touch, and in what order, and waits for you to approve, amend, or reject that plan before any of it executes. (Posit Assistant writes the plan to a Markdown plan file, and its documentation describes this as an instruction to the model rather than a hard lock, so still read what it does.) Plan shows you the intended shape of a whole multi-step job before a single file changes. It is the review gate for work too large to specify edit by edit but too consequential to hand straight to an autonomous agent.
The progression is one of widening autonomy with a review point inserted before the riskiest step:








Mode
What you get back
What changes
Your control point



Ask
Prose and code in the reply
Nothing
You apply everything by hand


Plan
An ordered plan of intended steps
Nothing, until you approve
You approve the plan before execution


Agent
Executed changes across the project
Files and state, as it works
You review the result, or the pull request



At the time of writing (October 2026), Plan mode is available in Copilot Chat in VS Code (choose Plan in the chat’s agent picker) and in Posit Assistant (type /plan). The natural workflow for any non-trivial agent task is Plan first, read the plan, then let it execute, rather than handing a goal straight to Agent mode and discovering its choices after the fact.


Plan, review, then execute


In Copilot in VS Code or Posit Assistant, with your forked repository committed and clean, switch to Plan mode and give it a goal that spans more than one step:
In the voles pipeline, add a derived mass_change column (mass_post_g minus
mass_pre_g) to the loading step, then create a new script that plots
mass_change by treatment_arm, and make sure the pipeline still runs end to
end.
Read the plan it returns before doing anything else. It should name the files it intends to touch, the order it will work in, and how it will check the pipeline. This is the moment to catch a wrong assumption: if it proposes editing the raw data, or putting the plot in the wrong place, or skipping the end-to-end check, you say so now, while nothing has changed. Amend the plan in conversation, then approve it and let it execute. Compare the experience with handing the same goal straight to Agent mode in Block 5: the difference is that you saw the intent before the action, not the action before the review.


Agent skills
A skill is a packaged procedure the assistant loads when a task calls for it, rather than a set of rules attached to a file type or applied to every request. For Copilot it lives in .github/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md (or .agents/skills/ or .claude/skills/) and carries a name and a description in its front matter; the description is what the assistant reads to decide the skill is relevant, or you invoke it directly by name. Because a skill loads only when needed, it can be longer and carry supporting material, templates, tables, and reference files that an always-on instruction file could not afford to include on every request.
A caution before the demonstration, following from the orientation at the start of this block. Skills are the one mechanism here that does not transfer cleanly across the tools, and this is why the skills exercise behaves differently from desk to desk:

GitHub Copilot loads skills from .github/skills/, .claude/skills/ or .agents/skills/. At the time of writing (October 2026), skills work with the cloud agent, Copilot code review, the Copilot CLI, and agent mode in VS Code; run the exercise below in Agent mode.
Posit Assistant loads skills automatically, but from its own list of locations: .agents/skills/ or .posit/assistant/skills/ in the project (older versions used .positai/), or other paths you add to skills.paths. It does not look in .github/skills/.

So the one project location both tools read is .agents/skills/. A skill placed under .github/skills/ reaches every Copilot surface but not Posit Assistant.
The skill demonstrated is pub-figures, which governs the production of every figure in the project that a human will read. It encodes a chart-selection table, a list of unconditional prohibitions (no pie charts, no dual y-axes, no dynamite plots when raw data are available), an accessible colour scheme, audience-specific styling, a mandatory colour-vision-deficiency check, and a checklist.






Warning



Run this exercise where the skill will actually load. With GitHub Copilot, that is agent mode, either in VS Code or with the cloud agent on GitHub.com, with the skill in .github/skills/pub-figures/. If you want to run it in Posit Assistant instead, move the folder to .agents/skills/pub-figures/; Copilot reads that location too, so one copy then serves both tools. The steps below are written for Copilot.


1. Default output. In a fresh Chat session (with no skill loaded), ask:
Produce a ggplot2 boxplot of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
dataset.
The result is a default-styled boxplot: grey background, ggplot2 default colours, no consideration of accessibility, no annotation of sample sizes. It runs and answers the literal question, and that is all.
2. With the skill. Open a new Chat session, select Agent mode, invoke the skill (/pub-figures), and ask the same question. The skill requires the agent to elicit the audience before producing code. It will ask whether the figure is for a journal or lab report, a poster, a talk, or public engagement. Answer “journal/lab report” and confirm the plan it produces.
The skill folder looks like this:
your-repo/
└── .github/
    └── skills/
        └── pub-figures/
            ├── SKILL.md
            ├── raincloud-template.R
            ├── emmeans-bridge.R
            ├── save-figure.R
            └── theme-project.R
The output is materially different. A raincloud (ggdist::stat_halfeye plus a boxplot plus jittered points) should replace the bare boxplot, because the skill specifies raincloud as the default for discrete-continuous comparisons where raw data are available. The palette is colour-blind friendly. Axis labels carry units. The pre-flight checklist is reported in the chat.
3. Iteration. Ask the agent to add pairwise statistical annotation. The skill prohibits hallucinating p-values, so the agent should refuse unless a fitted model object is available. Provide a fitted lm() and the emmeans contrasts; the agent will use ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual() to draw brackets and labels from the model-derived data. The four-element figure legend appears at the bottom of the output.
How to write skills
You will receive these skills rather than author them in this workshop, but it is worth seeing how a skill is built. The same structure applies when you write your own, it explains why the demonstration above behaved as it did, and it is the shape of the characterisation-test skill sketched (but not built) in Block 8.
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file, for example .github/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md or .agents/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md, with a YAML front-matter block and a Markdown body. Two parts decide whether it works:

The description in the front matter is the trigger. It is the text the agent reads to decide whether the skill is relevant to a request, so it must name the condition under which the skill applies, specifically. “Used when producing any ggplot2 figure a human will read” loads when it should; “for plots” loads erratically. A skill invoked by name with /skill-name does not depend on the description, but a skill you want loaded automatically does.
The body is a procedure: when to use the skill, the ordered steps, any hard prohibitions, and a final checklist. Because a skill is read only when invoked, it can be long without slowing ordinary interactions, which is why the pub-figures skill can carry a chart-selection table, a prohibition list, and an accessibility check at no cost to a routine question. Supporting files such as templates or reference tables can sit in the skill folder alongside SKILL.md.

Posit has published a series of skills on GitHub here. They are .md files with supporting templates, and they can be used with a range of LLM providers.

title: Block 7: AI-Assisted Code Review
text:
Part 1 — What AI is, and is not, good for in code review
⏱ ~15 minutes
On Day 2 you performed a manual 4Rs review. It was thorough but slow. The appeal of an AI reviewer is speed and recall: it reads every line, never tires, and flags the unused xgboost import you might skim past. The danger is the mirror image. It produces fluent, confident output that is sometimes wrong, and it is wrong in a specific, dangerous pattern.
Map AI capability onto the 4Rs you already know:
AI capability mapped onto the 4Rs

R
AI is...
Why



Reported
Good (for drafting)
It can summarise what the script appears to do and flag missing documentation, undocumented exclusions, and name drift. It cannot know the intended analysis unless you tell it.


Run
Strong
Typos (libray), absolute paths, unused or duplicated library() calls, and mis-spelled functions are exactly the surface features models detect reliably.


Reliable
Weak and dangerous
The silent semantic errors (P4 precedence, P8 sentinel, P9 incomparable models, P10 wrong family) are context-dependent. A model may catch some, miss others, and invent problems that are not there, all in the same confident register.


Reproducible
Mixed
It can flag a missing sessionInfo() or the ambiguous three-model situation. It cannot confirm results reproduce unless it can actually run the code.
The evidence supports this division of labour rather than wholesale delegation. When Google deployed an LLM-based reviewer of coding best practices to tens of thousands of developers, the share of its comments developers rated useful plateaued at around half, and the team had to suppress whole categories of non-actionable comments and tune confidence thresholds because otherwise the tool risked losing developers’ trust (Vijayvergiya et al. 2024). A detailed manual study of automated code-review tools found that each succeeds on some kinds of change and fails on others, and that a general-purpose LLM (ChatGPT) did poorly at writing review comments of the kind a human reviewer writes (Tufano et al. 2024). The practical consequence for you: treat every AI finding as a claim to verify, not a result to accept, and treat the absence of a finding as no evidence the bug is absent.

text:

A: Yes — it read every line B: Only if I had also read it myself C: No — I would trust my own review over the AI’s D: I would trust it for Run, not for Reliable
