title: Appendix A — R Basics
text:
A.11 Functions
Functions are the tools of R. Each one helps us to do a different task.
Take for example the function that we use to round a number to a certain number of digits - this function is called round.
Here’s an example:

round(x  = 2.4326782647, digits = 2)

We start the command with the function name round. The name is followed by parentheses (). Within these we place the arguments for the function, each of which is separated by a comma.
The arguments:

x = 2.4326782647 (the number we would like to round)
digits = 2 (the number of decimal places we would like to round to)

Arguments are the inputs we give to a function. These arguments are in the form name = value: the name specifies the argument, and the value is what we are providing to define the input. That is, the first argument x is the number we would like to round, it has a value of 2.4326782647. The second argument digits is how we would like the number to be rounded and we specify 2. There is no limit to how many arguments a function could have.






Tip



Copy and paste the following code into the console.



help(round)

The help documentation for round() should appear in the bottom right help panel. In the usage section, we see that round() takes the following form:

round(x, digits = 0)

In the arguments section, there are explanations for each of the arguments. x is the number or vector where we wish to round values. digits is the number of decimal places to be used. In the description we can see that if no value is supplied for digits it will default to 0 or whole number rounding.
Read the ‘Details’ section to find out what happens when rounding when the last digit is a 5.
Let’s try an example that leaves out the optional argument digits, so the default is used:






Tip



Copy and paste the following code into the console.



round(x  = 2.4326782647)

[1] 2


Now we can supply digits to produce a different result.

round(x  = 2.4326782647, digits = 2)

[1] 2.43


This time R has still rounded the number, but it has done so to a set number of ‘decimal places’.
Always remember to use the help documentation to help you understand what arguments a function requires.

A.11.1 Storing the output of functions
What if we need the answer from a function in a later calculation? The answer is to use the assignment operator again <-.
In this example we assign values to two R objects that we can then call inside our R function as though we were putting numbers in directly.






Tip



Copy and paste the following code into the console.



number_of_digits <- 3

my_number <- 2.4326782647

rounded_number <- round(x  = my_number, 
                        digits = number_of_digits)

What value is assigned to the R object rounded_number ?


Solution


[1] 2.433



A.11.2 More fun with functions
Copy and paste this:

round(2.4326782647, 2)

Looks like we don’t even have to give the names of arguments for a function to still work. This works because the function round expects us to give the number value first, and the argument for rounding digits second. But this assumes we know the expected order of arguments, which may be true for functions we use a lot. If you give arguments their proper names then you can actually introduce them in any order you want.
Try this:

round(digits = 2, x  = 2.4326782647)

But this gives a different answer:

round(2, 2.4326782647)







Warning



Remember: naming arguments overrides the default positions.


How do we know the argument orders and defaults? Well we get to know how a lot of functions work through practice, but we can also use help().

title: Appendix A — R Basics
text:
A.12 Packages
When you install R you will have access to a range of functions including options for data wrangling and statistical analysis. The functions that are included in the default installation are typically referred to as Base R and there is a useful cheat sheet that shows many Base R functions here
However, the power of R is that it is extendable and open source - anyone can create a new package that extends the functions of R.
An R package is a container for various things including functions and data. These make it easy to carry out complicated procedures with custom-built functions. Later we will see how we can write our own simple functions. Packages are a lot like new apps extending the functionality of what your phone can do.

A.12.1 Loading packages
To use the functions from a package in our script they must be loaded before we call on the functions or data they contain. So the most sensible place to put library calls for packages is at the very top of our script.

library(package_name)


A.12.2 Calling Functions from Packages
After loading a package, you can call its functions using either function() or the full package_name::function_name() syntax. The second form names the package explicitly.

library(dplyr)

filter(dataframe, condition)

dplyr::filter(dataframe, conditions)

Calling a function explicitly via its package can be useful for:

Avoiding Conflicts:

Sometimes, multiple packages may have functions with the same name. By explicitly specifying the package with package_name::, you avoid naming conflicts and ensure that R uses the function from the intended package.

Clarity:

It can make your code more transparent and easier to understand, especially in cases where the function’s origin is not immediately obvious. This is helpful for both yourself and others who read your code.

It is still good practice to note at the top of your script that the package is required, even if you don’t include library(package).


Debugging:

When troubleshooting issues or debugging code, specifying the package source of a function can help pinpoint problems and ensure that the correct function is being used.

A.12.3 Using packages
The tidyverse is an opinionated collection of R packages designed for data science. All packages share an underlying design philosophy, grammar, and data structures. This means the functions across the tidyverse are all designed to work together and make the process of data science easier.
Run the code below to load the tidyverse package.

library(tidyverse)

You will get what looks like an error message - it’s not. It’s just R telling you what it’s done. You should read this: it gives you a full list of the packages it has made available to you.
Now that we’ve loaded the tidyverse package we can use any of the functions it contains but remember, you need to run the library() function every time you start R.


Install the tidyverse (only needed if it is not already installed)

To use a package, you must first install it. The following code installs the package tidyverse, a package we will use very frequently.
If you are working on your own computer, use the code below to install the tidyverse.

install.packages("tidyverse")

You only need to install a package once. However, each time you start R you need to load the packages you want to use, in the same way that you install an app on your phone once but open it every time you want to use it.








Important



If you get an error message that says something like “WARNING: Rtools is required to build R packages” you may need to download and install an extra bit of software called Rtools.



A.12.4 Package updates
In addition to updates to R and RStudio, the creators of packages also sometimes update their code. This can be to add functions to a package, or it can be to fix errors. One thing to avoid is unintentionally updating an installed package. When you run install.packages() it will always install the latest version of the package and it will overwrite any older versions you may have installed. Sometimes this isn’t a problem, however, sometimes you will find that the update means your code no longer works as the package has changed substantially. It is possible to revert to an older version of a package, but it is better not to need to.






Important



To avoid accidentally overwriting a package with a later version, you should never include install.packages() in your analysis scripts in case you, or someone else, runs the code by mistake. Install packages from the console instead (or let renv manage them, as we do on Day 2).



A.12.5 Package conflicts
There are thousands of different R packages with even more functions. Unfortunately, sometimes different packages have the same function names. For example, the packages dplyr and MASS both have a function named select(). If you load both of these packages, R will produce a warning telling you that there is a conflict.

library(dplyr)
library(MASS)

Attaching package: 'dplyr'

The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag

The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union


Attaching package: 'MASS'

The following object is masked from 'package:dplyr':

    select
In this case, R is telling you that the function select() in the dplyr package is being hidden (or ‘masked’) by another function with the same name. If you were to try and use select(), R would use the function from the package that was loaded most recently - in this case it would use the function from MASS.
If you want to specify which package you want to use for a particular function you can use code in the format package::function, for example:

dplyr::select()
MASS::select()







Note



Why do we get naming conflicts?
This is because R is open source software. Anyone can write and submit useful R packages. As a result it is impossible to make sure that there are NEVER any functions with identical names.

title: Appendix A — R Basics
text:
A.13 Error
Things will go wrong eventually, they always do…
R is very pedantic: even the smallest typo can result in failure, and typos are impossible to avoid. So we will make mistakes. One type of mistake we will make is an error. The code fails to run. The most common causes for an error are:

typos
missing commas
missing brackets

There’s nothing wrong with making lots of errors. The trick is not to panic or get frustrated, but to read the error message and our script carefully and start to debug (more on this later)…
… and sometimes we need to walk away and come back later!






Tip



Try typing the command help() into the R console. It should open a new tab on the bottom right.
Put a function or package into the brackets to get help with a specific topic.






courtesy of Allison Horst

title: Appendix A — R Basics
text:
A.14 More on objects
A large part of your coding will involve creating and manipulating objects. Objects contain stuff, and we made our first R objects earlier in this chapter. The values contained in an object can be numbers, words, or the result of operations and analyses. You assign content to an object using <-.


Create some objects


Copy and paste the following code into the console, change the code so that it uses your own name and age and run it. You should see that name, age, today, new_year, and data appear in the environment pane.

name <- "emily"
age <- 16 + 19 
today <- Sys.Date()
new_year <- as.Date("2027-01-01")
data <- rnorm(n = 10, mean = 15, sd = 3)

What command should you use if you need help to understand the function rnorm()?







Objects in the environment



Note that in these examples, name,age, and new_year would always contain the values emily, 35, and the date of New Year’s Day 2027. However, today will draw the date from the operating system and data will be a randomly generated set of data so the values of these objects will not be static.
As a side note, if you ever have to teach programming and statistics, don’t use your age as an example because every time you have to update your teaching materials you get a reminder of the fragility of existence and your advancing age.
Objects can also be used in calculations and can interact with each other. For example:

age + 10
new_year - today
mean(data)

[1] 45
Time difference of 78 days
[1] 14.11677


Finally, you can store the result of these operations in a new object:

decade <- age + 10







Note



You may find it helpful to read <- as contains, e.g., name contains the text emily.


You will constantly be creating objects throughout this course and you will learn more about them and how they behave as we go along. For now it is enough to understand that they are a way of saving values, that these values can be numbers, text, or the result of operations, and that they can be used in further operations to create new variables.






Note



You may also see objects referred to as ‘variables’. There is a difference between the two in programming terms, but the words are very often used interchangeably.

title: Appendix A — R Basics
section: A.15 Making a tibble from scratch
text:
A.15 Making a tibble from scratch
We have looked at R objects that contain:

single elements of data
multiple elements of the same data type - vectors

But when we import data into R, it is most often put into an object called a tibble, which is a type of dataframe.






Note



A dataframe is a data structure that organises data into a table. Dataframes can have a mix of different types of data in them. Each column in a dataframe is a different vector, and each row is a different element within the vectors.


Let’s have another quick go at making our own tibble from scratch.

# make some variables/ vectors
person <- c("Mark", "Phil", "Becky", "Tony")

hobby <- c("kickboxing", "coding", "dog walking", "car boot sales")

awesomeness <- c(1,100,1,1)







Tip



Use str() on an object or vector to find out important information, like the data type of each vector and how many elements it contains.


Now we put these vectors together with the function tibble(), and they become the variables in a new tibble:

# make a tibble
my_data <- tibble(person, hobby, awesomeness)
my_data

title: Appendix A — R Basics
section: A.16 Organising data in wide and long formats
text:
A.16 Organising data in wide and long formats
There are two main conventions for dataframes in R: wide and long formats.

A wide data format does not repeat values in the first column, data relating to the same “measured thing” are found in different columns
A long data format is where we have a different column for each type of thing we have measured in our data. Each variable has a unique column.





A visual representation of long and wide format data shapes



While neither wide nor long data is more correct than the other, we will work with long data as it is clearer how many distinct types of variables there are in our data and the tools we will be using from the tidyverse are designed to work with long data.






Tip



Reshaping data between wide and long formats is covered in more depth in Appendix B.

title: Appendix A — R Basics
section: A.17 How to cite R and RStudio
text:
A.17 How to cite R and RStudio
You may be some way off writing a scientific report where you have to cite and reference R, however, when the time comes it is important to do so to give the people who built it (most of them for free!) credit. You should provide separate citations for R, RStudio, and the packages you use.
To get the citation for the version of R you are using, run the citation() function which will always provide you with the most recent citation.

citation()

To cite R in publications use:

  R Core Team (2025). _R: A Language and Environment for Statistical
  Computing_. R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria.
  <https://www.R-project.org/>.

A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is

  @Manual{,
    title = {R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing},
    author = {{R Core Team}},
    organization = {R Foundation for Statistical Computing},
    address = {Vienna, Austria},
    year = {2025},
    url = {https://www.R-project.org/},
  }

We have invested a lot of time and effort in creating R, please cite it
when using it for data analysis. See also 'citation("pkgname")' for
citing R packages.


To generate the citation for any packages you are using, you can also use the citation() function with the name of the package you wish to cite.

citation("tidyverse")

To cite package 'tidyverse' in publications use:

  Wickham H, Averick M, Bryan J, Chang W, McGowan LD, François R,
  Grolemund G, Hayes A, Henry L, Hester J, Kuhn M, Pedersen TL, Miller

  the tidyverse." _Journal of Open Source Software_, *4*(43), 1686.
  doi:10.21105/joss.01686 <https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.01686>.

A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is

  @Article{,
    title = {Welcome to the {tidyverse}},
    author = {Hadley Wickham and Mara Averick and Jennifer Bryan and Winston Chang and Lucy D'Agostino McGowan and Romain François and Garrett Grolemund and Alex Hayes and Lionel Henry and Jim Hester and Max Kuhn and Thomas Lin Pedersen and Evan Miller and Stephan Milton Bache and Kirill Müller and Jeroen Ooms and David Robinson and Dana Paige Seidel and Vitalie Spinu and Kohske Takahashi and Davis Vaughan and Claus Wilke and Kara Woo and Hiroaki Yutani},

To generate the citation for the version of RStudio you are using, you can use the RStudio.Version() function:

RStudio.Version()

Finally, here’s an example of how that might look in the write-up of your method section:

You may not have to do this for a while, but come back to this section when you do.

title: Appendix A — R Basics
text:
A.18 Help and additional resources




The truth about programming



Getting good at programming really means getting good at trying stuff out, searching for help online, and finding examples of code to copy. If you are having difficulty with any of the exercises contained in this book then ask the course instructors for help. However, learning to problem-solve effectively is a key skill that you need to develop throughout this course.

Use the help documentation. If you’re struggling to understand how a function works, remember the ?function and help() commands.
If you get an error message, copy and paste it into Google - it’s very likely someone else has had the same problem.
If you are struggling to produce a particular output or process - try organising your Google searches to include key terms such as “in R” or “tidyverse”. - e.g. “how to change character strings into NA values with tidyverse”
The official Cheatsheets are a great resource to keep bookmarked.
Remember to ask for help

In addition to these course materials there are a number of excellent resources for learning R:

StackOverflow
R for Data Science (2e)
The Posit Community forum

title: Appendix A — R Basics
text:
A.19 Debugging tips
A large part of coding is trying to figure out why your code doesn’t work and this is true whether you are a novice or an expert. As you progress through this course you should keep a record of mistakes you make and how you fixed them. In each chapter we will provide a number of common mistakes to look out for but you will undoubtedly make (and fix!) new mistakes yourself.

A.19.1 Prevent errors
Read console outputs as you go
Check that functions are producing the output you expect
Build complex code in simple stages

A.19.2 Fix errors

Have you loaded the correct packages for the functions you are trying to use? One very common mistake is to write the code to load the package, e.g., library(tidyverse) but then forget to run it.
Have you made a typo? Remember data is not the same as DATA and t.test is not the same as t_test.
Is there a package conflict? Have you tried specifying the package and function with package::function?
Is it definitely an error? Not all red text in R means an error - sometimes it is just giving you a message with information.

title: Appendix A — R Basics
text:
A.20 Test yourself
Question 1. Why should you never include the code install.packages() in your analysis scripts? 
You should use library() instead
Packages are already part of Base R
You (or someone else) may accidentally install a package update that stops your code working
You already have the latest version of the package


Explain This Answer


Remember, when you run install.packages() it will always install the latest version of the package and it will overwrite any older versions of the package you may have installed.


Question 2. What will the following code produce?

rnorm(6, 50, 10)


A dataset with 10 numbers that has a mean of 6 and an SD of 50
A dataset with 6 numbers that has a mean of 50 and an SD of 10
A dataset with 50 numbers that has a mean of 10 and an SD of 6
A dataset with 6 numbers that has a mean of 10 and an SD of 50


Explain This Answer


The default form for rnorm() is rnorm(n, mean, sd). If you need help remembering what each argument of a function does, look up the help documentation by running ?rnorm


Question 3. If you have two packages that have functions with the same name and you want to specify exactly which package to use, what code would you use?

package::function
function::package
library(package)
install.packages(package)


Explain This Answer


You should use the form package::function, for example dplyr::select. Remember that when you first load your packages R will warn you if any functions have the same name - remember to look out for this!

title: Appendix B — Tidy data
text:
B.1 Why tidy data?
We are going to learn how to organise data using the tidy format, because this is the format the tidyverse packages Wickham (2023) are built around. The tidyverse is an opinionated but highly effective approach to reproducible analysis, with a wide range of data manipulation tools. Tidy data is an easy format for computers to read. It is also the structure that most modelling and plotting functions in R expect.
Here ‘tidy’ refers to a specific structure that lets us manipulate and visualise data with ease. In a tidy dataset each variable is in one column and each row contains one observation. Each cell of the table/spreadsheet contains the values. You might notice that tidy data is quite long: it has a lot of rows. This is why tidy data is also called long-format data (as opposed to wide data).

title: Appendix B — Tidy data
text:
The data cleaning and analysis tools in R work best with data that is “tidy”
“Tidy” data has a clear and consistent structure; untidy data can be “messy” in lots of different ways

title: Appendix B — Tidy data
text:
B.2 Using pivot functions
What do we do if the data we are working with in R isn’t “tidy”?
The tidyverse includes functions that help us reshape data:

tidyr::pivot_wider() - from long to wide format
tidyr::pivot_longer() - from wide to long format





Reshaping data with pivot




 country <- c("x", "y", "z")
 yr1960 <-  c(10, 20, 30)
 yr1970 <-  c(13, 23, 33)
 yr2010 <-  c(15, 25, 35)

country_data <- tibble(country, yr1960, yr1970, yr2010)
country_data

B.2.1 Pivot longer

pivot_longer(data = country_data,
             cols = yr1960:yr2010,
             names_to = "year",
             names_prefix = "yr",
             values_to = "metric")





Reshaping data with pivot



To save these changes to your data format, you must assign the result to an object. You have two options:

Use the same name as the original R object: this will overwrite the original with the new format
Use a new name for the reformatted data: both R objects will then exist in your Environment

Neither is more correct than the other but be aware of what you are doing.

B.2.2 Create a new r object

long_country_data <- pivot_longer(data = country_data,
             cols = yr1960:yr2010,
             names_to = "year",
             names_prefix = "yr", # optional
             values_to = "metric")


B.2.3 Overwrite the original object

country_data <- pivot_longer(data = country_data,
             cols = yr1960:yr2010,
             names_to = "year",
             names_prefix = "yr",
             values_to = "metric")

After running this, country_data is in long format, so the wide-format code above will no longer work on it (the yr1960:yr2010 columns are gone). This is why we created long_country_data first.

B.2.4 Pivot wider
Let’s use the long country data we have just generated as an example of how we could use the pivot_wider() function and reverse the process:

pivot_wider(data = long_country_data,
            names_from = year,
            names_prefix = "yr",
            values_from = "metric")

title: Appendix C — Joins
text:
C.1 Join functions
Data analysis often requires merging separately managed tables back together. There are multiple ways to join the observations in two tables, based on how the rows of one table are merged with the rows of the other.
When thinking about joins, picture two tables, one on the left and one on the right. The most common (and often useful) join is when you merge the subset of rows that have matches in both the left table and the right table: this is called an INNER JOIN. Other types of join are also possible:
There are also two filtering joins, which keep or drop rows of the left table without adding any columns from the right table:
We will use two small example tables. They share an ID column, which we tell each join to match on with join_by() (dplyr 1.1.0 and later; older code uses by = "ID").
# Create tibbles df_primary and df_secondary
df_primary <- tibble(
  ID = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "F"),
  y = c(5, 5, 8, 0, 9)
)

df_secondary <- tibble(
  ID = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  z = c(30, 21, 22, 25, 29)
)

title: Appendix C — Joins
text:
A LEFT JOIN takes all of the rows from the left table, and merges on the data from matching rows in the right table. Rows in the left table with no matching key are still kept, with a missing value (NA) for the right table’s columns.
A RIGHT JOIN is the same, except that all of the rows from the right table are included with matching data from the left, or a missing value.
Finally, a FULL JOIN includes all data from all rows in both tables, and includes missing values wherever necessary.



A SEMI JOIN keeps the rows of the left table that have a match in the right table.
An ANTI JOIN keeps the rows of the left table that have no match in the right table. This is very handy for finding records that are missing from a lookup table.

inner_join(df_primary, df_secondary, join_by(ID))

In this chapter, we will:
To put these ideas into practice, we’ll use the penguins dataset from palmerpenguins, because I like penguins.
PROS: Why gt? Has a grammar of tables, like ggplot2, supports HTML, LaTeX and RTF, follows tidyverse conventions.

title: Appendix D — Making tables with gt
text:
D.1 Conclusion
Many of the tweaks we made to our table are quite subtle. Changes like removing excess gridlines, bolding header text, right-aligning numeric values, and adjusting the level of precision can often go unnoticed, but if you skip them, your table will be far less effective. Our final product isn’t flashy, but it does communicate clearly.
We used the gt package to make our high-quality table, and as we’ve repeatedly seen, this package has good defaults built in. Often, you don’t need to change much in your code to make effective tables. But whichever package you use, give tables as much thought as any other kind of data visualisation.
You can put these tables straight into a Quarto document (see the Quarto block on Day 3), where they render as part of your report.

text:
E.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Data visualisation helps us see relationships, patterns and surprises that tables of numbers can easily hide. In this chapter, we’ll use ggplot2{Wickham et al. (2026)}, part of the tidyverse, to build clear graphics step by step.

Download penguin data (RDS)

text:
Understand the basic structure of a ggplot and how it builds layer by layer.
Map data variables to visual aesthetics like position, colour and shape.
Add and customise plot elements such as labels, themes, and titles.
Use facets to compare subgroups effectively.
Apply best practices for clear, meaningful visualisations.









Note

The penguins data used here is loaded from files/chapter5.RDS (download it below and read it in with readRDS()). It keeps the original column names from the raw Palmer data, so bill measurements are called culmen_length_mm and culmen_depth_mm. title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
Building plots
We’ll be using the ggplot2 package to create data visualisations. It’s part of the tidyverse suite of packages. Although many people refer to it simply as ggplot, its official name is ggplot2.


ggplot2 uses a layered grammar of graphics, where plots are constructed through a series of layers. You start with a base layer (by calling ggplot), then add data and aesthetics, followed by selecting the appropriate geometries for the plot.
These first 3 layers give you the simplest version of a complete plot. You can then make the plot clearer and better looking by adding further layers such as scales, facets, coordinates, labels and themes.

Let’s build a basic scatterplot to show the relationship between flipper_length and body_mass. We will customise the plots further in later sections; for now, this gives a quick overview of the different layers.


Layer 1 creates the base plot that we build upon.

Layer 2 adds the data and some aesthetics:

The data is passed as the first argument.
Aesthetics are added via the mapping argument, where you define your variables (e.g., x or both x and y). This also lets you specify general properties, like the colour for grouping variables.



Layer 3 adds geometries, or geom_? for short. This tells ggplot how to display the data points. Remember to add these layers with a +, rather than using a pipe (|> or %>%). You can also add multiple geoms if needed, for example, combining a violin plot with a boxplot.

Layer 4 includes scale_? functions, which let you customise aesthetics like colour. You can do much more with scales, but we’ll explore that later.

Layer 5 introduces facets, such as facet_wrap(), allowing you to add an extra dimension to your plot by showing the relationship you are interested in for each level of a categorical variable.

Layer 6 involves coordinates, where coord_cartesian() controls the limits for the x- and y-axes (xlim and ylim), enabling you to zoom in or out of the plot.

Layer 7 helps you modify axis labels.

Layer 8 controls the overall style of the plot, including background colour, text size and borders. R provides several predefined themes, such as theme_classic, theme_bw, theme_minimal, and theme_light.

Click on the tabs below to see how each layer contributes to refining the plot.


Layer 1
Layer 2
Layer 3
Layer 4
Layer 5
Layer 6
Layer 7
Layer 8




ggplot()







There’s not much to see at this stage - this is basically an empty plot layer.



ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm))







You won’t see any data points yet because we haven’t specified how to display them. However, we have mapped the aesthetics, indicating that we want to plot body_mass on the x-axis and flipper_length on the y-axis. This also sets the axis titles, as well as the axis values and breakpoints.






Tip



You don’t need to include data = or mapping = if you keep those arguments in the default order. Similarly, the first column name you enter in the aes() function will automatically be interpreted as the x variable, and the second as y, so you can omit specifying x and y if you prefer.

ggplot(penguins, aes(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm))

will give you the same output as the code above.





ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point()







Here we are telling ggplot to add a scatterplot. You may notice a warning indicating that some rows were removed due to missing values.
The colour argument adds colour to the points based on a grouping variable (in this case, sex). If you want all the points to be black (showing only two dimensions rather than three), omit the colour argument.



ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  # changes colour palette
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + 
  # add breaks from 2500 to 6500 in increasing steps of 500
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(from = 2500, to = 6500, by = 500)) 







The scale_? functions allow us to modify the colour palette of the plot, adjust axis breaks, and more. You could change the axis labels within scale_x_continuous() as well or leave it for Layer 7.



ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm, colour=sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + 
  # split main plot up into different subplots by species 
  facet_wrap(~ species) 







In this step, we’re using faceting to split the plot by species.



ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm, colour=sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + 
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  # limits the range of the y axis
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 250)) 







Here we adjust the limits of the y-axis to zoom out of the plot. If you want to zoom in or out of the x-axis, you can add the xlim argument to the coord_cartesian() function.



ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm, colour=sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + 
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(x = "Body Mass (in g)", # labels the x axis
       y = "Flipper length (in mm)", # labels the y axis
       colour = "Sex") # labels the grouping variable in the legend







You can change the axis labels using the labs() function, or you can modify them when adjusting the scales (e.g., within the scale_x_continuous() function).



ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm, colour=sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + 
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(x = "Body Mass (in g)", 
       y = "Flipper length (in mm)",
       colour = "Sex") +
  # add a theme
  theme_classic()







The theme_classic() function is applied to change the overall appearance of the plot.









Important



You need the first three layers to create your base plot. Everything else is optional, so you don’t need to use all eight layers. Layers 4-8 can be added in any order (more or less), whereas layers 1-3 must follow a fixed sequence.

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.2 Exploring Common Geom Types
So far we have only made a scatterplot, but ggplot offers many more geoms. This chapter works through some of the most common ones.







Data type
Example geom
Purpose



Continuous–continuous

geom_point(), geom_line(), geom_smooth()

Relationships/trends


Categorical–continuous

geom_boxplot(), geom_violin(), geom_col()

Comparisons


Continuous

geom_histogram(), geom_density()

Distributions

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.3 Histogram (geom_histogram())
If you want to show the distribution of a continuous variable, you can use a histogram. As with every plot, you need at least 3 layers to create a base version of the plot. Like geom_bar(), geom_histogram() only requires an x variable as it does the counting “in the background”.
A histogram divides the data into “bins” (i.e., groupings displayed in a single bar). These bins are plotted along the x-axis, with the y-axis showing the count of observations in each bin. It’s basically a barchart for continuous variables.
Let’s have a look at the weight distribution in our dataset.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram() 






Figure E.1: Default histogram




The default number of bins is 30 (as shown in Figure E.1 above). Changing the number of bins (argument bins) makes the histogram coarser or finer. More bins show more detail.
Perhaps it’s more intuitive to modify the width of each bin using the binwidth argument. For example, binwidth = 1 for the weight category would mean each “weight group” represents 1 g, while binwidth = 50 would group weights into 50 g spans. The plots below show modifications for both bins and binwidth.

#less finetuning
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10) 

# more fineturning
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) 








Figure E.2: Bins vs binwidth arguments




The warning message tells us 2 rows of data were removed due to containing non-finite outside the scale range. Have a look at the body mass column (penguins) to see if you can decipher the warning message.
The rows were removed because 
they fall outside of the plot range
they contain missing values.
Click through each tab to see how you can modify colours, axis labels, margins, and breaks, and apply a different theme.


Colour
Axes labels, margins, and breaks
Themes



We can change the plot colours by adding a fill argument and a colour argument. The fill argument changes the colour of the bars, while the colour argument modifies the outline of the bars. Note that these arguments are added directly to the geom_histogram(), rather than within the overall aes(), because we want every bar to be the same colour rather than mapping colour to a variable.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE")













Tip



You could use:

Hex codes for fill and colour, as we did here: geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE"). If you want to create your own colours, check out this website.
Pre-defined colour names: geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "purple", colour = "green"). See the full list here.





Here we removed the label for the y-axis Count (to show you some variety) and modified the breaks. The y-axis is now displayed in increasing steps of 5, and the x-axis has a break every 500 g.
Notice how the breaks = argument changes the labels of the break ticks but not the scale limits. You can adjust the limits of the scale using the limits = argument. To make the effect obvious, we set the limits to 2000 and 7000. See how the values from 2000 to 2500, and 6500 to 7000 do not have labels? You would need to adjust that using the breaks = argument.
The expansion() function removes the gap between the x-axis and the bars.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE") +
  labs(x = "Body mass in (g)", # renaming x axis label
       y = "") + # removing the y axis label
  scale_y_continuous(
    # remove the space below the bars (first number), but keep a tiny bit (5%) above (second number)
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    # changing break points on y axis
    breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 5)
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    # changing break points on x axis
    breaks = seq(from = 2500, to = 6500, by = 500),
    # Experimenting with the scale limits
    limits = c(2000, 7000)
    )









Let’s experiment with the themes. For this plot we have chosen theme_bw():

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE") +
  labs(x = "Body mass in (g)", # renaming x axis label
       y = "") + # removing the y axis label
  scale_y_continuous(
    # remove the space below the bars (first number), but keep a tiny bit (5%) above (second number)
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    # changing break points on y axis
    breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 5)
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    # changing break points on x axis
    breaks = seq(from = 2500, to = 6500, by = 500),
    # Experimenting with the scale limits
    limits = c(2000, 7000)
    )+
  theme_bw()

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.4 Scatterplot (geom_point())
Scatterplots are appropriate when you want to plot two continuous variables. We can also add a trendline by using geom_smooth(). The default trendline is loess. If you want a linear trendline, you would need to add method = "lm" inside the geom_smooth() function.

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)








Figure E.3: Default Scatterplot with added trendline - loess (left) and linear (right)




Customising the colour of a scatterplot is slightly different from the other plots we’ve encountered so far. Technically, the point is not a “filled-in black area” but rather an extremely wide outline of a circle. Therefore, we cannot use the usual fill argument and instead need to use the colour argument, similar to how we customised the outline of the histogram.
See the tabs below to learn how to change the colour for all points or how to adjust the colour based on groupings.


Colour for all points
Colour with grouping
Legend title and labels



If we want to change the colour of all the points, we can add the colour argument to the geom_point() function. Likewise, to change the colour of the trendline, we would also use the colour argument. Here, we used pre-defined colour names, but HEX codes would work just as well.

# colour of all points and the trendline
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(colour = "darkorange")+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "darkblue")









If we want the points to change colour based on another grouping variable, the colour argument should go inside the aes(). If you don’t want to define the colours manually, you can use a colour palette like Brewer (scale_colour_brewer()) or Viridis (scale_colour_viridis_d()).

## adding grouping variable species and changing the colour values manually
ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple"))













ImportantWhat happened to the direction of correlation?





Colouring the points by species reveals a reversal of the apparent correlation.
This is known as Simpson’s Paradox, and is a result of “Omitted Variable Bias”: our original scatterplot did not include the confounder, species.
Omitting important variables can lead to incorrect conclusions.





You can tidy the legend title and group labels using the scale_colour_? function, depending on the palette you’re using (e.g., scale_colour_manual(), scale_colour_brewer and many more).

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple"),
                      name = "Species",
                      labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin"))












Your turn


All other layers remain exactly the same as in other plots. Try adding layers to make the plot above prettier:

1. relabel axes x and y
2. move the legend to a different position (either top, left, or bottom)
3. add a theme







NoteMore hints





If you are experiencing issues with the legend position and theme, try modifying the order of the layers.





Solution


ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              show.legend = FALSE)+ # stop this layer from appearing in the legend.
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple"),
                      name = "Species",
                      labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin"))+
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")+
  theme_classic() + # place before moving the legend position
  theme(legend.position = "top") # move legend to the top

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.5 Boxplot (geom_boxplot())
A boxplot is one way to display a continuous variable with a categorical grouping variable.

# default boxplot
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g))+
  geom_boxplot()







Tada! As usual, we can enhance the plot by adding various layers. Click on each tab below to see how.


Colour
Axes labels
Legend and Theme



We can change the colour by adding a fill argument inside the aes(). To customise the colours further, we can add a scale_fill_? layer. If you have specific colours in mind, use scale_fill_manual(). If you prefer pre-defined palettes, such as Brewer, you can use scale_fill_brewer().

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  # customise colour
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2")









We need to relabel the axes. The function to use depends on the variable type. Here, we need scale_x_discrete() for the x-axis and scale_y_continuous() for the y-axis. We can also tidy up the group labels and adjust the breaks on the y-axis (e.g., in steps of 500 g) within these same functions.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2")+
  scale_x_discrete(
    # changing the label of x
    name = "Species",
    # changing the group labels of the 3 groups
    labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    # changing name of the y axis
    name = "Body mass (g)",
    # changing break labels
    breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500))
  )









The legend is superfluous; best to take it off. We can remove the legend by adding the argument guide = "none" to the scale_fill_? function.
Let’s pick a theme we haven’t used yet: theme_dark().

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2",
                    guide = "none")+
  scale_x_discrete(
    # changing the label of x
    name = "Species",
    # changing the group labels of the 3 groups
    labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    # changing name of the y axis
    name = "Body mass (g)",
    # changing break labels
    breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500))
  ) +
  theme_dark()

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.6 Violin plot (geom_violin())
An alternative way to display a continuous variable with a categorical grouping variable is a violin plot.

# default violin plot
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin()









Your turn


Adjusting the violin plot would be exactly the same as the boxplot. Try to add layers to the base plot above to:

change the colours either manually or using a pre-defined colour palette
tidy the axes labels and group names
in case a legend appears, take it off
add a theme



Solution


ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin()+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2",
                    guide = "none")+
  scale_x_discrete(
    # changing the label of x
    name = "Species",
    # changing the group labels of the 3 groups
    labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    # changing name of the y axis
    name = "Body mass (g)",
    # changing break labels
    breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500))
  )+
  theme_bw()

title: Appendix E — ggplot
text:
E.7 Violin-boxplots
So far, we’ve only added one geom_? layer to our plots. However, thanks to ggplot’s layered system, we can add multiple geoms, for example, when creating a violin-boxplot.
Remember, the order of the layers can sometimes make a difference. We’ve seen this already - adding a theme at the end can override earlier arguments like the legend position. Similarly, ggplot + violinplot + boxplot will look different from ggplot + boxplot + violinplot.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin()+
  geom_boxplot()


ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_violin()








Figure E.4: Default violin-boxplot: Order of the layer matters




See the tabs below to learn how to customise various elements, such as the width of the boxes, and the colour or opacity.


Width of the boxes
Colour



If we want to get any information from the boxplot, we need to place it “on top of” the violin plot. But still, the boxplot is pretty wide and covers important details from the violin plot. To make the information more visible, we can adjust the width of the boxes. Finding an appropriate width might take some trial and error.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin()+
  geom_boxplot(width = .2)






Figure E.5: Default violin-boxplot: adjusting width of the box






Adding colour should be pretty straightforward by now. The code is no different from what we used for the boxplot or violin plot. We need to add the fill argument within the aes(), along with a scale_fill_? layer.
However, we can further customise the plot by adding an opacity argument using alpha to the violin plot geom.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) + # alpha for opacity
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) + # change width of the boxes
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") # customise colour






Figure E.6: Violin-boxplot with a different colour palette









Your turn



Change the x- and y-axis labels
Remove the legend
add a theme



Solution


ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
    geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2",
                    guide = "none")+
  scale_x_discrete(
    # changing the label of x
    name = "Species",
    # changing the group labels of the 3 groups
    labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    # changing name of the y axis
    name = "Body mass (g)",
    # changing break labels
    breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500))
  )














Meyer, F., & Perrier, V. (2025). Esquisse: Explore and visualize your data interactively. https://dreamrs.github.io/esquisse/


Wickham, H., Chang, W., Henry, L., Pedersen, T. L., Takahashi, K., Wilke, C., Woo, K., Yutani, H., Dunnington, D., & van den Brand, T. (2026). ggplot2: Create elegant data visualisations using the grammar of graphics. https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
Prepare and summarise data for advanced plotting.
Control aesthetics and grouping behaviour in multilayered plots.
Use and combine a broad range of geoms, including line and label.
Customise and extend colours, palettes, scales, axes, and legends.
Use facets effectively for multi-dimensional comparisons.
Arrange and enhance plots using patchwork and marginal plots.
Export visualisations with ggsave() and make them interactive with plotly.







Note



Like Appendix E, this appendix uses the penguins data from files/chapter5.RDS, which keeps the original culmen_length_mm and culmen_depth_mm column names (called bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm in palmerpenguins::penguins and on Day 3).

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.2 Colours, palettes and extensions
Colour is one of the strongest visual cues in data visualisation. In ggplot2, colours can mark categories, highlight relationships and guide the viewer’s attention. It is also one of the most common sources of confusion and inaccessibility.

F.2.1 How colour works in ggplot2

ggplot2 applies colour in two main ways:

Mapped colour: controlled by a variable in aes(), such as colour = species or fill = species.
Fixed colour: set manually outside aes(), e.g. geom_point(colour = "blue").


penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()









Your turn



Change the code above so that all the points are coloured blue.



Solution


penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g))+ 
  geom_point(colour = "blue")








The colour argument needs to go inside the relevant geom(), as only aes is inherited across layers.

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.3 Choosing Effective Palettes






Tip



Choosing palettes and checking them for colour vision deficiency are covered in more depth in Day 3, Block 1 (Colour and Accessibility) and Block 4 (Accessible colour with colorspace and colorBlindness).


Good palettes show contrast and group differences, and stay readable for all audiences.
In ggplot2, colours that are assigned to variables are modified via the scale_colour_* and the scale_fill_* functions. To use colour with your data, the most important thing to know is whether you are dealing with a categorical or continuous variable. Choose the colour palette according to the type of variable:

sequential or diverging colour palettes for continuous variables
qualitative colour palettes for (unordered) categorical variables









You can pick your own sets of colours and assign them to a categorical variable. The number of specified colours has to match the number of categories. You can use a wide range of preset colour names or you can use hexadecimals.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 20, 
               alpha = 0.7, 
               position = "identity") +
scale_fill_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
theme_minimal()








F.3.1 Using Predefined Palettes from colorspace
The colorspace Ihaka et al. (2025) package offers curated, perceptually balanced palettes designed for clarity and accessibility.
You can select qualitative, sequential, or diverging palettes using scale_*_discrete_qualitative(palette = "*") or similar functions.

library(colorspace)

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
scale_fill_discrete_qualitative() +
theme_minimal()









Your turn


Explore the palettes available in colorspace:

Run the command hcl_palettes(plot = TRUE)
Choose an appropriate palette and try it for our plot



Solution


library(colorspace)

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
theme_minimal()











F.3.2 Other palettes

Generate a palette
Wes Anderson palettes
ggokabeito
scico

F.3.3 Accessibility
It’s very easy to get carried away with colour palettes, but your figures must always be accessible. One way to check how accessible your figures are is to use a colour blindness checker, colorBlindness Ou (2021).

## Check accessibility ----

library(colorBlindness)
colorBlindness::cvdPlot() # will automatically run on the last plot you made








F.3.4 Guides to visual accessibility
Using colours to tell categories apart can be useful, but as we can see in the example above, you should choose carefully. Other aesthetics you can use in your geoms include shape and size, and you can combine these with colour to make your plots more accessible. Here is a hierarchy of “interpretability” for different types of data:










Shape
Colour
Colour redundancy




penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             shape=species))+ 
  geom_point() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(21,22,23))










penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) 










penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species,
             shape = species))+ 
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3"))

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.4 Grouping logic
When drawing lines with geom_line(), ggplot2 needs to know which points belong together.
If it cannot infer groups, it will connect every point in order of x, producing meaningless zigzags.
Let’s see how grouping works implicitly, explicitly and in summary form.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
    geom_line()








F.4.1 Implicit grouping via colour or fill
Discrete aesthetics such as color, fill, or linetype automatically define groups.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
color = species)) +
  geom_line()








F.4.2 Explicit grouping
Explicit grouping defines the groups by which lines should be drawn (still in order of x) without relying on other aesthetics or implicit grouping.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
group = species)) +
  geom_line()








ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
colour = species, group = individual_id)) +
  geom_line()








F.4.3 Summary trend lines

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm,
colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha =.8)+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.5 Scales, Axes and Ordering

F.5.1 Axes limits
Now, we’ll use scale_x_continuous() and scale_y_continuous() for setting our desired values on the axes.
The key parameters in both functions are:

“limits” (defined as limits = c(value, value))
“breaks” (which represent the tick marks, specified as breaks = value:value).

Note that “limits” are only two values (the minimum and maximum), while “breaks” are a range of values (for instance, from 0 to 100).

## Set axis limits ----
penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,240), 
                     breaks = seq(20,240,by = 20))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,7000), 
                     breaks = seq(0,7000,by = 10))









Your turn


Pick a more appropriate set of axis breaks:


Solution

R chooses the limits and breaks for you automatically. But it is useful to know how to override this when needed.

## Set axis limits ----
penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(160,240), 
                     breaks = seq(160,240,by = 20))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2500,6500), 
                     breaks = seq(2500,6500,by = 500))











F.5.2 Zooming in and out
We have seen how we can set the parameters for the axes for both continuous and discrete scales.
It can be useful to zoom in and out of figures, mainly to focus on one section of the plot.
One function we can use to do this is coord_cartesian() in ggplot2, where you can:

Set the limits on the x-axis (xlim = c(value, value))
Set the limits on the y-axis (ylim = c(value, value))
Set whether to add a small expansion to those limits or not (expand = TRUE/FALSE).


penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(180,210), 
                  ylim = c(3000,4000), 
                  expand = FALSE)













ImportantLimits vs co-ords





This IS different to setting the axis limits. coord_cartesian is like a zoom, while scale sets the plotting range.
Below we use a shortcut to scale with xlim and ylim - the trendline is now calculated only from the visible/plotted points.

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", 
                             "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", 
                             "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) +
  xlim(180,210) +
  ylim(3000,4000)











F.5.3 Axis ordering
Axis ordering affects how quickly and accurately viewers can interpret data.
For example, ordering categories by value shows which groups have the highest or lowest measurements, while random or inconsistent ordering makes comparisons confusing.
By default R will order categories along the axis in alphabetical order:

penguins |> 
ggplot(aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar()













NoteQuestion



What makes the default ordering less than suitable for rapid comparisons?



F.5.3.1 Reordering manually
To switch the order, use the scale_x_discrete() function and set the limits within it (limits = c(“category”,“category”)):

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar()+
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Adelie", "Gentoo","Chinstrap")) 








F.5.3.2 Reordering by values
Or by using features in the forcats package:

fct_infreq(): orders by frequency
fct_reorder(): orders by another numeric variable (e.g., mean body mass)


penguins |> 
  mutate(species = forcats::fct_infreq(species)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar()









Your turn


How could we improve the readability of this plot even further?


Solution


penguins |> 
  mutate(species = forcats::fct_infreq(species)) |> 
  # Species on the y axis gives horizontal bars, which are easier to read
  ggplot(aes(y = species)) +
  geom_bar()+
  # Direct annotation
  geom_label(stat='count', aes(label=after_stat(count)))+
  # reverse order so the most common species is at the top
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev)+
  # Redundant titles removed
  labs(y = "",
       x = "Count")

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.6 Facets
When it becomes difficult to see the trends or differences in your plot, we can break up a single plot into sub-plots; this is called ‘faceting’. Facets are commonly used when there is too much data to display clearly in a single plot.

F.6.1 Cluttered plots
In the example below it is hard to see the exact distribution of each histogram:

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g,
             fill = species))+
  geom_histogram()+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))







Facetted panels make side-by-side comparisons easier:

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g,
             fill = species))+
  geom_histogram()+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+
  facet_wrap(~species) # make facets by species

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.7 Highlighting
Plot highlighting, for example with the gghighlight package in R Yutani (2025), lets you:

Emphasise values over certain ranges
Emphasise key groups
Make facetted plots easier to read:


library(gghighlight)

penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g,
             fill = species))+
  geom_histogram(position = "identity")+
  gghighlight()+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+
  facet_wrap(~ species)








F.7.1 Nested Facets
The ggh4x::facet_nested() function in the ggh4x van den Brand (2025) package is used for creating nested or hierarchical faceting in ggplot2 plots. Nested faceting lets you subdivide facet panels into smaller panels, creating a hierarchy of facets.

library(ggh4x)

penguins |> 
  mutate(Nester = ifelse(species=="Gentoo", "Crustaceans", "Fish & Krill")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = culmen_length_mm,
             y = culmen_depth_mm,
             colour = species))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_nested(~ Nester + species)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.8 Patchwork
patchwork Pedersen (2025) lets you combine multiple ggplots, side by side or stacked, without exporting to another program.
This keeps everything reproducible inside R.

Use / to stack plots vertically
Use + to align plots horizontally


library(patchwork)

p1 <- penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = culmen_length_mm))+
  geom_point(aes(colour=species))+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))

p2 <- penguins |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=culmen_depth_mm, 
             y = culmen_length_mm))+
  geom_point(aes(colour=species))+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))


p3 <- penguins |>     
     drop_na(sex) |> 
     ggplot(aes(x=species, 
                fill = sex)) + 
    geom_bar(width = .8,
             position = position_dodge(width = .85))+
  scale_fill_discrete_diverging()

 (p1+p2)/p3+
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") 







You can also add overall titles and adjust layouts:

 (p1+p2)/p3+
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
plot_annotation(
title = "Penguin Bill and Body Measurements",
subtitle = "Comparing relationships across species"
)








F.8.1 Marginal plots
A marginal plot augments a two-dimensional plot (usually a scatterplot) with one-dimensional summaries along its margins, typically histograms, density curves, or boxplots.
They let readers inspect the joint relationship and each variable’s distribution simultaneously.
Conceptually:

The main panel shows how x and y relate.
The marginal panels show the univariate spread of each variable.


pal <- c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan")

# density plot of flipper length
marginal_1 <- penguins |>  
  ggplot()+
  geom_density(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, fill = species),
               alpha = 0.5)+
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal)+
  theme_void()+
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# density plot of body mass
marginal_2 <- penguins |>  
  ggplot()+
  # body mass on y, so the density runs vertically beside the scatterplot
  geom_density(aes(y = body_mass_g, fill = species),
               alpha = 0.5)+
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal)+
  theme_void()+
  theme(legend.position = "none")


scatterplot <- penguins |>  
  ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, 
             y = body_mass_g,
             colour=species))+ ### now colour is set here it will be inherited by ALL layers
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm",    #add another layer of data representation.
              se=FALSE)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal)+
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Layout allows us to have total customisation over the position of our plots

layout <- "
AAA#
BBBC
BBBC
BBBC"


marginal_1+scatterplot+marginal_2 +plot_layout(design = layout)

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.9 Plotly
plotly Sievert et al. (2025) turns static ggplots into interactive web graphics built on the JavaScript Plotly.js library. It preserves ggplot2’s grammar (via ggplotly()), but turns each layer into a responsive SVG/HTML element with tooltips, zooming, and panning:

library(plotly)
ggplotly(
penguins |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = culmen_length_mm,
            y= body_mass_g,
            colour = species)) +
    geom_point(aes(fill = species), shape = 21, colour = "white") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,linetype = "dashed", alpha = .4)+
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))
)

title: Appendix F — ggplot2
text:
F.10 Exporting safely

F.10.1 ggsave







Tip



Saving figures is covered in more depth in Day 3, Block 5 (Saving figures correctly).


One of the easiest ways to save a figure you have made is with the ggsave() function. By default it will save the last plot you made on the screen.
You should specify the output path to your figures folder, then provide a file name. Here I want to save it as a .PNG image file. Always set the width, height, units and resolution (dpi) explicitly: the defaults depend on the size of your plot window, so the same code can produce a different figure each time. dpi 300 is good enough for most purposes.

# OUTPUT FIGURE TO FILE


ggsave("outputs/figures/YYYYMMDD_ggplot_workshop_final_plot.png",
       width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300)


F.10.2 svg

Not exactly programmatic, but occasionally a lifesaver. If you save your ggplot image in .svg format then it becomes vectorised.
What does this mean?
Open your image in a programme like PowerPoint and each element of the plot can be edited, resized or moved!

ggsave("outputs/figures/test-file.svg",
       width = 7, height = 5, units = "in")

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
text:
G.1 Why a data frame is sometimes the wrong tool
Throughout this chapter we use the Portal mammals survey data, distributed as both a CSV file and a SQLite database. The CSV is around 35,000 rows: small enough to inspect, large enough to make timing differences visible.
A data.frame (and its tidyverse refinement, the tibble) holds the whole dataset in memory and copies it on most operations. For tens of thousands of rows this is invisible. For tens of millions it becomes the dominant cost of an analysis, and for data larger than available RAM it fails outright.
Two strategies address this. The first keeps the data in memory but uses a structure optimised for speed and low copying: data.table. The second leaves the data on disk in a database and pulls only what each query needs: a SQLite file queried through dbplyr. The rest of this chapter works through each in turn.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
text:
Note



The thresholds are approximate and hardware-dependent, but a useful rule of thumb: under ~1 GB, a tibble is fine; from ~1 GB up to the limits of RAM, reach for data.table; beyond RAM, or when the data are already in a database, use a database backend.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
text:
G.2 Reading large files: fread()

There are three common ways to read a delimited file: base R’s read.csv(), readr::read_csv(), and data.table::fread(). For small files the choice is immaterial. As files grow past roughly 100 MB the differences become substantial, with fread() and read_csv() typically several times faster than read.csv().

library(microbenchmark)

microbenchmark(
  base  = read.csv(csv_name),
  readr = readr::read_csv(csv_name, show_col_types = FALSE),
  dt    = data.table::fread(csv_name, showProgress = FALSE),
  times = 10,
  unit  = "ms"
)

The return types differ, and this matters. read.csv() returns a data.frame, read_csv() returns a tibble, and fread() returns a data.table. The first two behave identically for our purposes; the data.table is a different object with its own syntax, covered below.

G.2.1 Reading only part of a file
When a file does not fit in memory, the simplest fix is to read less of it. fread() exposes two arguments for this. nrows caps the number of rows read, and skip discards rows from the top or, given a string, starts reading at the first line matching it.

# First 500 rows only
fread(csv_name, nrows = 500, showProgress = FALSE)

# Start from the first line containing "1986"
fread(csv_name, skip = "1986", showProgress = FALSE)

The select argument restricts which columns are read, which often has a larger effect on memory than restricting rows. drop is its complement.

three_columns <- fread(
  csv_name,
  select       = c("species_id", "sex", "hindfoot_length"),
  showProgress = FALSE
)

readr offers the same controls under different names: n_max for rows, skip for an offset, and col_select for columns. Unlike older versions, col_select now accepts column names directly, so the two packages are close to equivalent here.

readr::read_delim(
  csv_name,
  delim      = ",",
  n_max      = 500,
  col_select = c(species_id, sex, hindfoot_length)
)

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
section: G.3 data.table syntax in one minute
text:
G.3 data.table syntax in one minute
A data.table is indexed as dt[i, j, by]: filter rows in i, do something to columns in j, grouped by by. It is terse and fast, but the grammar is not dplyr’s.

allData <- fread(csv_name, showProgress = FALSE)

# Filter rows
allData[year > 1988]

# Select columns (note: .() returns a data.table, not a vector)
allData[, .(species_id, year)]

# Aggregate by group
allData[, .(mean_hf = mean(hindfoot_length, na.rm = TRUE)), by = species_id]

You do not have to learn this grammar to get the speed. dtplyr lets you write ordinary dplyr and translates it to data.table code under the hood.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
section: G.4 Driving data.table with dplyr: dtplyr

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
section: G.5 When the data live on disk: databases
text:
G.5 When the data live on disk: databases
data.table still holds everything in memory. Once the data exceed RAM, or when they already sit in a shared database, the better move is to leave them where they are and query across the connection. We use SQLite here because it is a single file with no server to configure, but the same code works against PostgreSQL, MySQL, BigQuery, and others through the common DBI interface.

library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

# A connection to a SQLite database file
mammals <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(),
                          here::here("data", "portal_mammals.sqlite"))

DBI::dbListTables(mammals)
# [1] "plots"   "species" "surveys"

dbConnect() opens the connection; RSQLite::SQLite() names the driver. The returned object, mammals, is the handle we query against. Point a tbl() at one of its tables to get something that behaves like a lazy tibble.

surveys <- dplyr::tbl(mammals, "surveys")
surveys
# # Source:   table<`surveys`> [?? x 9]
# # Database: sqlite [.../portal_mammals.sqlite]
#    record_id month   day  year plot_id species_id sex   ...
#        <int> <int> <int> <int>   <int> <chr>      <chr>
#  1         1     7    16  1977       2 NL         M
#  ...

Note the [?? x 9]: R reports nine columns but an unknown number of rows. It has not counted them, because doing so would mean reading the whole table. This laziness is the point: R fetches only what a query needs.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
text:
G.6 Querying with dbplyr

dbplyr translates dplyr verbs into SQL automatically. In practice you write the same pipeline you would for a local tibble, with one addition: nothing is fetched until you call collect().

library(dbplyr)

# How many males were recorded in plot 2 in 1978?
surveys |>
  filter(sex == "M", year == 1978, plot_id == 2) |>
  count() |>
  collect()                # <- pulls the result into a local tibble

Without collect(), the pipeline remains a query object and prints only a preview. With it, the SQL runs on the database and the (usually small) result comes back as an ordinary tibble you can plot or model. Filter and aggregate on the database side, where the data are; collect() only the reduced result.






Note



Most dplyr verbs translate, but not all of R is available inside a database. slice_head() and friends are unsupported because database tables have no inherent row order, and any function dbplyr cannot translate will error. When that happens, collect() first and finish the work locally.



G.6.1 Seeing the generated SQL
Learning what dbplyr produces is a low-cost way to learn SQL itself. Pipe any un-collected query into show_query().

surveys |>
  filter(year %in% c(1998, 1999, 2000)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(year, species_id)) |>
  show_query()
# <SQL>
# SELECT `year`, `species_id`, COUNT(*) AS `n`
# FROM `surveys`
# WHERE (`year` IN (1998, 1999, 2000))
# GROUP BY `year`, `species_id`

If you prefer to write SQL directly, DBI::dbGetQuery() sends a raw query and returns a data frame in one step.

DBI::dbGetQuery(
  mammals,
  "SELECT year, species_id, COUNT(*) AS n
   FROM surveys
   WHERE year IN (1998, 1999, 2000)
   GROUP BY year, species_id"
)


G.6.2 Activity: SQL to dplyr and back


read it, then write it


First, translate this SQL into a dbplyr pipeline:
SELECT record_id, hindfoot_length
FROM surveys
WHERE hindfoot_length > 20
Then, going the other way, write the dbplyr pipeline below, predict the SQL it will generate, and check your prediction with show_query():

surveys |>
  filter(year > 1977, year < 2000, hindfoot_length == 30) |>
  arrange(desc(species_id))





Solution


# SQL -> dbplyr
surveys |>
  select(record_id, hindfoot_length) |>
  filter(hindfoot_length > 20) |>
  collect()

# The second pipeline generates SQL along these lines:
# SELECT *
# FROM `surveys`
# WHERE (`year` > 1977 AND `year` < 2000 AND `hindfoot_length` = 30)
# ORDER BY `species_id` DESC

Two things to notice. The chained filter() conditions become a single WHERE joined by AND, and arrange(desc(...)) becomes ORDER BY ... DESC. The mapping is close enough that reading SQL and reading dplyr reinforce each other.

title: Appendix G — Working with larger data
section: G.7 Building a database from a CSV
text:
G.7 Building a database from a CSV
If your data start life as a CSV that is too large to load, you can write it into a SQLite file in chunks, then query it lazily as above. Read a block with fread(), append it to the table, and repeat. purrr::walk() drives the loop for its side effect (writing), returning nothing.

library(purrr)

db <- dbConnect(SQLite(), here::here("data", "surveys.sqlite"))

# Read the column names once, from the header line only
col_names <- names(fread(csv_name, nrows = 0))
n <- 5000

# Write one chunk: skip the header plus `skip_rows` data rows, read `n` rows,
# and append them to the table
write_chunk <- function(skip_rows) {
  chunk <- fread(csv_name, skip = skip_rows + 1, nrows = n, header = FALSE,
                 col.names = col_names, showProgress = FALSE)
  dbWriteTable(db, "surveys", chunk, append = TRUE)
}

# Offsets for each chunk (the file has 35,549 data rows), then write them all
skips <- seq(0, by = n, length.out = 8)
walk(skips, write_chunk)

dbDisconnect(db)

Only the first line of the file holds the column names, so we read them once and pass them to every chunk with header = FALSE. Without this, every chunk after the first loses its names and dbWriteTable() refuses to append it. The + 1 in skip steps over that header line. The general pattern is to never hold more than one chunk in memory at a time.






Note



Where this leaves us. We can read selectively with fread(), run dplyr at data.table speed through lazy_dt(), and query on-disk databases through dbplyr while fetching only what we need with collect(). The common thread is that the dplyr grammar carries across all three settings; what changes is where the data sit and when the work actually runs.
